I had this prepared by treasury board. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked how it was that Mr. Conway was appointed or commenced work on April 21, the day before the government itself was sworn in.
Under the financial arrangements made with Mr. Conway he was entitled to a living
2386	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry allowance for each day he was absent from his normal place of residence, and a professional fee for each day he was engaged in his duties with the Department of Finance. In addition, he was entitled to receive transportation expenses.
The pertinent regulations provide that entitlement to a per diem living allowance commences when a person leaves his normal place of residence en route to the new location where he will be performing his duties. Mr. Conway left his normal place of residence, which was Boston, by air at 7 p.m. on Sunday, April 21, in order to start work in Ottawa on Monday, April 22. Mr. Conway was entitled to, and received, for April 21 reimbursement of his transportation expenses, which commenced with his journey from Boston on April 21, and reimbursement for one half day's living allowance for April 21. He had to spend the night here. His professional fee did not commence until April 22.
Because Mr. Conway was entitled to, and received, reimbursement for travelling and living expenses incurred on April 21, that date was given as his commencement date. Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. There have been


discussions on this subject between the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. There have been a number of reports from abroad which were highly inaccurate, particularly in their references to the possible role of Canada in relation to this matter. This decision was taken by the former government in January of this year, and it was reaffirmed by Canada to the United Kingdom in the month of June. I can assure the house that the military, political and economic considerations were exhaustively studied by the Canadian government before it reached the decision and before there was confirmation of that decision. Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1.	That with respect to new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired in the period of 24 months commencing June 14,	1963 capital cost
allowances be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum if the property has been acquired by a taxpayer in a taxation year for a manufacturing or processing business in Canada and the taxpayer is
(a)	an individual who was resident in Canada for a period of not less than 183 days in the year, or
(b)	a corporation that in the year had a degree of Canadian ownership and control;
and for the purposes of this paragraph,
(c)	a corporation has a degree of Canadian ownership and control in a year if the corporation throughout the 60 day period immediately preceding the year (or if the corporation did not have a preceding year, throughout the 60 day period commencing on the first day of the year) complied with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation was resident in Canada,
(ii)	either
(A)	not less than 25 per cent of its voting shares were beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof,
or
(B)	the voting shares of the corporation were listed on a recognized stock exchange in Canada and it is established, in prescribed manner, that no one non-resident shareholder owned beneficially, together with any other person associated with him at any time in the period, more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation, and
(iii)	where the year commences after December 31, 1964, the number of directors of the corporation who were resident in Canada was not less than 25 per cent of the total number of directors of the corporation;
or complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i) and (iii) and was a wholly-owned subsidiary of a corporation that throughout the 60 day period complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i), (ii) and (iii); and

(d)	a corporation is controlled in Canada at a particular time if at that time it complies with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation is resident in Canada, and
(ii)	not less than 51 per cent of its voting shares are beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof.
2.	That a taxpayer whose business in a prescribed area of Canada has been certified to be a new manufacturing or processing business that commenced commercial operations in the period of 24 months commencing with the date on which any enactment based on this paragraph is assented to be exempt from tax on the income from that business for a period of 36 months from the date certified to be the date of commencement of operations, and that the rate of capital cost allowances for new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired by the said taxpayer in the said 24 months period for such business be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum.
3.	That with effect for 1964 and subsequent taxation years section 40A of the act, which provides for a deduction from the tax otherwise payable by a manufacturing and processing corporation, be repealed.

That with respect to expenses incurred after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by it on or in respect of exploring for petroleum or natural gas in Canada and the prospecting, exploration and development expenses incurred by it in searching for minerals in Canada.

(a)	is taxable as a non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada,
(b)	derives substantially all of its income from sources in Canada, and

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I appreciate the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman. I am prepared to go on now with the income tax resolutions. The officials who are familiar with that side of things are here. I suggest that with any luck we will get through the income tax resolution very quickly, and then we will be in a position to go on with the excise tax resolution this afternoon.
You are a great believer in luck.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I don't know why. The income tax resolution sets forth a number of proposals which are now to be considered in turn on the basis of their individual merits. These were described in the budget speech. Although the measures were amended and clarified by the statement made on July 8, the basic principles and purposes are unaltered.
Since there are 23 numbered paragraphs it may assist hon. members of the committee at this stage to recapitulate in a few sentences the broad areas of subject matter to which the proposals are directed. Substantial tax incentives to encourage industrial growth and employment in the country at large and additional incentives for particular designated areas of slower growth are set forth in paragraphs 1 and 2. The repeal provision in paragraph 3 may be considered in connection with these.
An incentive measure affecting drilling and exploration for gas and oil is summarized in paragraph 4. Measures designed to exert an influence on the ownership of Canadian industry are set forth in paragraphs 1, 6 and 7. Other paragraphs which are either consequential or closely related to these are Nos. 5 and 8 and Nos. 9 to 12 inclusive.

A measure designed to encourage certain non-resident institutions to invest in Canadian bonds is contained in paragraph 13. If the hon. member will wait a moment, I was just going to add that this, of course, will be partially but by no means wholly upset, in fact not to more than a degree, if the present Kennedy proposals are passed by congress. The provision still offers a very important inducement to certain investors in the United States to buy Canadian bonds.
A measure to obtain earlier payment of corporation income taxes and to enhance the flow of revenues during the next two years is contained in paragraphs 14 and 15. Measures to achieve greater equity by closing loopholes and by improving the administration of the Income Tax Act are set forth in paragraphs 16 to 23 inclusive, and I expect that hon. members of the committee will be very interested in those proposals.
I will, of course, give an introduction to each of the main paragraphs in the resolution when we come to them, and with the approval of the committee I should like to begin with an introduction to paragraph 1. This paragraph provides a tax incentive for manufacturing and processing businesses with a degree of Canadian ownership and control. The paragraph proposes that accelerated capital cost allowances be granted in respect of certain new depreciable property acquired in a 24 month period for use in manufacturing and processing businesses by individuals resident in Canada or by companies resident in Canada that have a degree of Canadian ownership and control.
A taxpayer acquiring new machinery or equipment that would otherwise fall in class 8 of the Income Tax Act regulations for use in a manufacturing or processing business will be allowed to claim capital cost allowances in respect of that machinery or equipment at the rate of 50 per cent on a straight line basis. This 50 per cent rate is a maximum rate. Taxpayers may spread the deduction of capital cost allowances over a number of years if they so wish.
When capital cost allowances are calculated on a straight line basis a fixed percentage of the original capital cost may be deducted each year until the total capital cost has been deducted for tax purposes. For example, under the concession referred to here 50 per cent of the capital cost will be deducted in the first year and 50 per cent in the second. This method compares with the diminishing balance basis which is the general rule under Canadian tax law.
The normal capital cost allowance for machinery and equipment is 20 per cent on the diminishing balance basis; that is, if a machine costs say $1,000 an amount of $200
Income Tax Act
would be deductible in the first year, and in the second year 20 per cent of the remaining balance or $160 would be deductible. In the third year $128 would be deductible, and so on. Under the proposed incentive the cost of machinery may be deducted over a period of two years whereas under the normal rules only about two thirds of the cost of the machinery would be deducted by the end of the fifth year.
I mention this because the extent of this incentive is very great indeed, and in the opinion of the government it will mean a great speed up in investment in the private sector of the economy in the next two years. In order to qualify for the accelerated allowance-
That is the thing; qualification.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not qualification. I think the word "qualify" is clear enough. In order to qualify for the accelerated allowance the machinery and equipment must be acquired by the taxpayer in the period commencing June 14, 1963 and ending June 13, 1965. That is the nature and the extent of the incentive, and I think it is fair to say that this incentive is greater and will probably have more important results than any other incentive that I can recall of this kind.
The requirements which a company must meet to have a degree of Canadian ownership and control are contained in detail in the resolution. First, the company must be a resident of Canada. Second, there are certain requirements concerning ownership of the company's shares which must be met. On this point companies have a choice between two tests. Test A is that no less than 25 per cent of the company's voting shares must be beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or by a combination thereof. Test B is that the voting shares of the company must be listed on a stock exchange in Canada, and a non-resident company or an individual alone or with associated persons must not beneficially own more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the company. In other words there will be at least 25 per cent of the stock available for Canadian investors.
The third condition is that at least 25 per cent of the directors of the company must be resident in Canada, but this requirement does not apply until 1965, the purpose being to give companies a chance to meet the requirement. It is not normal to change directors in the course of a year.
This portion of the reference also provides that a company which is the wholly owned subsidiary of a company that qualifies as

Income Tax Act
having a degree of Canadian ownership and control shall also qualify, provided it is resident in Canada, and four years commencing after 1964 at least 25 per cent of its directors are resident in Canada. Now, obviously a time must be established for measuring or determining whether a company has a degree of Canadian ownership and control. A company will be regarded as having a degree of Canadian ownership and control during a taxation year if, during the period-this is the whole period-of 60 days immediately preceding that year it meets the stipulated requirement. For the first taxation year of a new corporation, its period is the first 60 days in that taxation year.
Subparagraph (d) of the first paragraph defines what is meant by a corporation controlled in Canada for the purposes of this provision.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is generally agreed, and it is a course that has been followed throughout the years on the first item of the resolution in committee stage, that a general discussion is permissible not only of the particular section but also of the entire field. Then as time goes on the individual items are dealt with as they come up. I mention that because the minister spoke with bland optimism of the hope that if we could get through this measure this afternoon we could proceed with other items. I would think this particular resolution is one that, on the basis of the reaction of Canadians generally and people abroad, deserves the fullest consideration and examination by parliament. Naturally the official critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, will deal in detail with these various matters.
However, I thought that it might be appropriate, in order to get a background for the discussion, to consider the courses that were outlined by the minister in the budget and the reaction that has resulted therefrom, not only within our own country but particularly abroad. I mention this because you will recall that for several years the Liberal party, then in opposition and also during the two recent elections, spoke most critically of the attitude taken by the previous government. They said we were anti-American when we took the stand we were pro-Canadian. Never in the widest stretch of our imagination would we have thought of bringing in the kind of legislation suggested by the present government, knowing full well the detrimental effect such would have not only on Canada and its economic advancement but as well on our relations with the United States.
The purpose of several of these resolutions is to interfere in Canada with foreign investment. Never did we at any time take

such a stand. We wanted to see as many as possible Canadian industries Canadianized. We wanted as well to assure that United States business subsidiaries coming into Canada should adopt an attitude of responding to Canadian objectives rather than having their course determined in a foreign country, however friendly. But they said we were antiAmerican when, in taking a stand on behalf of Canada, we endeavoured to bring about generally by conversations or arguments the objectives that the present government now says can only be brought about by legislation so drastic that already Canada's economy has been aversely affected.
You will recall, sir, the manner in which the various members of the present government maligned us, condemned us, pilloried us as anti-American. Never at any time did we even consider the possibility of going as far as this government has gone, because we had received our advice from trained civil servants. We knew what the effects would be. However, for some reason this government rushed in. I am not placing responsibility on the Minister of Finance. He is just the tribune for the rest of them. He gave them the plan and that plan has had, as I said a moment ago, a tremendously detrimental effect upon Canada's economy and upon Canada's image abroad. I intend to refer later to some of the recent editorials. I was pictured as one who would bring about a disruption in the wonderful relations with the United States that the previous government had enjoyed. Read the editorials today. All over the United States they are saying, in effect, nothing could be worse than what we have today in Canada. We are surprised; we are shocked. The Hyannis Port honeymoon is apparently over.
There was to be a new field of operations, a new spirit of Canadian-United States relations. They spoke of these things. In the budget they did everything they could to undo the possibility of good relations with that country. We believe in a strong Cana-dianism. We have said that. But, sir, what has been the effect? Does anyone think President Kennedy did not have before him a plan when he made the announcement yesterday? Had not Canada given him ample proof of ways that could be followed to bring about not an expansion of trade but a reduction, not an expansion of investment but a grave diminution?
As a matter of fact, on the basis of President Kennedy's message yesterday I do not think the Minister of Finance could have brought about the objectives he enunciated in the budget speech as effectively as the Kennedy plan will.

I wonder to what degree yesterday's drastic action on the part of the United States was in some way made excusable by the inexcusable measures that were proposed by the Minister of Finance in the budget. We believe in the objective of Canadian owned industry. We have taken that stand throughout, but these provisions as to the percentage of voting shares beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, and one or more corporations controlled in Canada, are as ineffectual in the administrative field as was the 30 per cent securities tax of unlamented memory.
They called it a face the facts budget, and now Canada faces the music as a result of the action taken yesterday. I do not know what manner of men brought about the various items in this connection, and I am referring particularly to those that deal with the need of Canadianizing Canadian industry; but on the basis of the last few weeks there is no Canadian who can deny that the chronology of the budget has been a continuing record of disaster unparalleled in Canada's parliamentary history.
It is a record of haphazard incompetence. The budget, and a number of these sections to which particular reference will be made, are the product of a government without a plan and without direction. The budget has been called everything, including a blunder budget and the vanishing budget. There are various sections in the Income Tax Act resolutions that I believe should also be withdrawn. They should be reconsidered, because they represent ill digested economic consideration of the effects that would follow such drastic, and in part quite ineffective, legislation.
When strong protests were made there was retreat. There are equally strong protests being made against various sections of these resolutions, and on the basis of those objections I think it would have been infinitely better for the government not to have engaged in a series of irresponsible declarations, followed by irretrievable retreats, but to have proceeded slowly and with full consideration. The government wanted to do all these things in a matter of a few days, but it was not the speed with which it operated that brought these economic monstrosities into being, because all of them were set forth in the book written by the minister.
But, sir, what has been the effect? Yesterday the President of the United States, in a special message to congress, asked for an immediate new excise tax ranging from 2J per cent to 15 per cent on the purchase of securities issued in 22 industrialized countries, and this tax is to remain in effect until
Income Tax Act
December 31, 1965. Yesterday the Prime Minister said he did not accept the suggestion on my part that Canada was the most affected country, but all across the nation, yesterday and this morning, the stock exchanges have indicated that Canada is the one nation most affected as a result of this action.
Where was this wonderful spirit of consultation that was developed at Hyannis Port? Yesterday the Prime Minister said "Oh, Canada was put in a special position; Canada was advised yesterday morning as to what was going to be done." Well, Mr. Chairman, the pressmen of the United States were given full information at least 12 hours before Canada was even considered.
What was Canada's reaction? What did the government say to the United States in the face of this drastic plan? What will be the effect? One of the principle items in United States newspapers over the last few weeks has been a suggestion that in view of the unbelievable action taken by the Canadian government, which was supposed to be superfriendly to the United States, retaliatory measures would have to be taken by the United States. I am not saying that what has been done is in that classification, but I recall the fact that in 1962, in the month of May, when we found it necessary to take economic action in regard to our foreign exchange, and when in June 1962 we borrowed from the international fund and took drastic action because of our international exchange difficulties, these magicians opposite said that what was being done represented the results of incompetence on the part of the then government.
What do they say about the United States now? Is this the result of incompetence? Is it the dilatoriness of the Kennedy administration that brought about the situation in respect of which action was taken yesterday? How they talked about incompetence on the part of the former government, but do they apply the same adjectival exaggeration to the Kennedy administration which had to take action yesterday, and which sees the most powerful nation in the world having to secure a grant of $500 million from the international monetary fund?
What is Canada's position now? Can she raise any objection to what is being done in the United States Can she argue that there should be some alleviation? Can she point out that we have the greatest trade with the United States, both ways, of any country in the world, and that therefore there should be some consideration given to Canada? No one would now advance that argument after the attitude implicit in the action taken by the government in its budget.

Income Tax Act
I would very much like to know the degree by which American antipathy has been materially increased as a result of the proposed 30 per cent tax on stock sales to foreign investors. Even though ridiculed by members of the present government, our relations with the United States over the last few years were on good terms, but we did not bow to demands on the part of the United States as to what we should do, and we did not fly in the face of the United States as did this government. I cannot understand why these supermen who sit opposite, these workers of economic magic, had no idea what the consequences would be of the totally inexcusable action taken in the budget in various particulars. That it was inexcusable is shown by the fact that the government turned tail and ran for cover on its 30 per cent takeover tax. I am hoping that the minister and the government, having established an unenviable record of declaration and retreat, will even now before this debate is over be prepared to suspend consideration of several of these items which cannot but have a detrimental effect on Canada's economy.
What is going to be the result of this? Administratively it will create chaos. I would like to know how the 25 per cent is going to be determined, on which day of the year it will apply. How are we going to police this without a tremendous bureaucracy? The very thought answers itself. I submit that in the philosophy of the budget, instead of it being one to provide for an expanded economy it has been a crippling one, slowing down economic activity. As a matter of fact only yesterday Mr. Kierans, the president of the Montreal stock exchange, had something to say about this. He is no friend of this party, but is close enough to the Liberal party to be a prospective Liberal candidate for election to the legislature of Quebec in support of Mr. Lesage-

ended.

That may not mean that he has too close a relationship with the government. He said that the action taken yesterday by President Kennedy, if it is approved and adopted by congress, will slow down economic activity, will hinder ready access to United States capital markets and will bring about higher interest rates. What happened yesterday was an understandable consequence of the government's attitude in this budget.
I am not saying it was the result of it at all; far from it, but it gave to the United States an object lesson as to what could be done between friendly nations. I repeat what I said earlier-
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the right hon. gentleman a question. Is this the explanation that he thinks the United States will make to the United Kingdom?
I do not care what explanation they may have made to the United Kingdom. I am thinking of Canada-United States relations.
Hear, hear.
I am glad to see this. It is one of the first times that the United Kingdom has been brought into debate in this house by representatives of the Liberal party as an example of what Canada should do.
Oh, oh.

I am dealing with Canada. The United Kingdom had nothing to do with the kind of nonsense that was embalmed in these resolutions and in the budget. I am speaking about what this government did by way of providing an object lesson to the United States as to action that might be taken. It is the most serious situation, according to John Meyer, that we have ever faced in this nation; and he is one who is quoted with respect, his opinion at all times being given full regard.
I know the government will not like my saying this, but I think I may generalize, without going into particulars, by simply saying that they instituted measures in the budget with no idea, apparently, of what the consequences would be. They instituted measures that were completely oblivious of the possibility of retaliatory measures being instituted. We cannot say anything to the United States now; we cannot say "Well, now, this thing is wrong; this is unfair; this is going to have a detrimental effect upon our economy". Five hundred and eighty million dollars have been invested in Canada by the United States since January 1 this year. That investment will certainly be materially reduced. Municipalities across Canada desiring to borrow in New York will find themselves unable to do so. Yet when the question was asked yesterday it was brushed aside as if it were of no particular consequence. Furthermore I suggest that in what is being done in general there is a violation by the present government of the spirit of the tax convention. What we have done by the threat inherent in the budget is to compromise Canada's position.
I am going to leave in a moment, Mr. Chairman, because I have a luncheon engagement. I simply summarize what I have been trying to say. The philosophy inherent in this budget is not in keeping with our relations with the United States. It is dangerous to the economic strength of this country; nobody can deny that. No matter how they would salve it over, the fact remains. I believe

in Canada determining its own destiny, in a Canada in which investment coming into this country shall be used for the purposes of Canada and not on the basis of the determination of any other country, however friendly. I say that when this is taken together, the whole philosophy, the packet plan as it were, it is a philosophy that cannot but have the effect psychologically and economically of interfering with Canada's growth and expansion. Instead of being a budget to help us develop, to give Canadians a new sense of adventure, to build up equality of opportunity in all parts of Canada, the philosophy in the 1963 budget is the antithesis of the idealistic objectives that were set out by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the Leader of the Opposition has dealt with a number of subjects in a rather general1 way and has sought, it seemed to me, to suggest that the particular budget resolutions which we are considering had such far reaching effects that they influenced President Kennedy in making his statement to congress yesterday, I thought it might be helpful to hon. members of the committee and to the public, perhaps through the press, to remind hon. members of just what this message from the President deals with and what it is trying to accomplish.
It seems to me that perhaps some hon. members have not had an opportunity to read and fully study the message, and there were moments when I wondered whether the right hon. gentleman opposite had really fully appreciated the implications of what the President was setting out to do. The message the President sent to congress is entitled "Special message on the balance of payments". The proposal for an interest equalization tax is only one of ten points that he brings to the attention of congress, and I would point out that he devotes only about one tenth of his message to this particular subject. It is one of a number of means by which the U.S. administration hope to improve their over-all balance of payments.
There can be no argument, of course, that the U.S. balance of payments has been weak and that it needs to be strengthened. In his message the president, as always, outlines various weaknesses and various means to overcome them. I suggest to all hon. members that we in Canada can be glad that the United States is taking steps to improve its international position and to ensure the continuing strength of the United States dollar. The greater part of world trade, after all, is conducted in United States dollars, and it is by far the world's major reserve currency. Anything that may disturb the flow of world
Income Tax Act
trade or may undermine international confidence is bad for a country like Canada with such a huge stake in international trade and international investment.
The United States balance of payments has in recent years been weak in an over-all sense, and it has been weaker in some directions than in others. While the United States has been running a substantial deficit, certain other countries have been running a corresponding surplus. While the United States has been losing gold reserves, other countries have been acquiring them. The major surplus countries are those in western Europe, and they include France, Germany and Italy in particular. It is in these countries that interest rates are substantially higher than they are in the United States.
In his introductory paragraphs on the interest equalization tax the President refers- and I quote his words-to-

Nor would it make sense, I suggest, if they were so intended to apply to Canada, because the fact of the matter is that Canada, so far from being a surplus country in this context, is as we all know, and we know it with regret, a deficit country. This country has run an international deficit for more than a decade, I think entirely with the United States. The deficit which we run bilaterally with the United States is even larger than our over-all deficit, because in our case we happen to run a surplus with overseas countries. Year by year we paid over to the United States foreign exchange that we had earned overseas. In other words the United States, far from running a deficit with Canada, has in fact been running a substantial surplus with us, and year in and year out we have used capital that we have raised in the United States to pay that country for the surplus of goods and services which we import from them.

While the net capital inflows from the United States to Canada in recent years have been very large, they have been less than our current account deficits with that country.
Under these conditions the United States would surely not wish to cut down their capital exports to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was saying, or suggesting, at one o'clock that while I was sure the Leader of the Opposition had not made any such suggestion the suggestion has been made that this proposed tax which was recommended by the President of the United States stems from, or is even in retaliation against, the alterations in the withholding tax which this committee is about to discuss.
This suggestion, if there is such a suggestion, can only be based on a misunderstanding of the nature of the alterations which the government is proposing. On balance, what we propose involves a substantial reduction, not an increase in our resident withholding tax. The tax is reduced immediately from 15 per cent to zero in relation to Canadian securities purchased by tax-free bodies in the United States and elsewhere. It is reduced immediately from 15 per cent to 10 per cent on income paid by corporations offering to Canadians at least a 25 per cent participation in their equity and directorate. The increase from 15 per cent to 20 per cent would only apply to corporations which, after the lapse of two and a half years, still do not offer Canadians that degree of participation. On balance, I repeat, we are proposing to reduce, not increase, our withholding tax.
Even if the United States were considering retaliation, and even if there were something to retaliate against, which of course there is not, I cannot conceive that any great and responsible nation would take measures against 22 countries, including its principal allies in the free world, in order to affect only one of them. To suggest any such thing would be the height of naivete, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands aptly pointed out yesterday.
In his message, the President indicates the priority to be given to the United States interest equalization tax. I quote:
I have been assured that the house ways and means committee will be prepared to give high priority to this proposal after action has been taken with respect to the over-all program of tax reduction and reform now before it.
On this basis, having in mind that congress will be considering this proposal after it has dealt with this somewhat controversial question of tax reduction, it is my understanding that it will be weeks, perhaps months, before action can be expected on this measure. In the meantime, we shall have ample opportunity to discuss with our United States friends the possible effects of the interest equalization tax not only on the Canadian financial system but also on our economy as a whole and on our balance of trade and

payments. In this connection I should like to quote a paragraph from the joint communique issued on May 11 at the end of the Hyannis Port meeting to which the right hon. gentleman referred earlier between the president and our Prime Minister.
The President and the Prime Minister stressed the interest of both countries in the balance of payments between them and with the rest of the world. The Prime Minister drew particular attention to the large United States surplus in the balance of current payments with Canada and noted the importance of allowing for this fact in determining the appropriate policies to be followed by each country. It was agreed that both governments should always deal in a positive and cooperative manner with developments affecting their international trade and payments.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members of this committee that this is the spirit in which we should approach this particular measure which the president has proposed and put before congress.

Mr. Chairman, 22 countries of the world are being subjected at the moment or at least in the future to that tax on imports of American capital into their countries. That 15 per cent tax was announced yesterday and we learned about it in the house yesterday afternoon. Today we could witness the reaction. The countries of the world who are proud of their liberties and of their national sovereignty did not see lit to express the reaction that we, in Canada, have displayed.
I would compare the situation to that of a new born infant. For some time, he thrives on his mother's milk but at a certain age, he is considered old enough to feed himself and he is weaned. Then he is left to develop by himself through his own efforts. build an enormous industrial empire without help, when we are still dependant on American finance?
Mr. Chairman, contrary to what others may think, in view of the fact that we have been unable to fend for ourselves, I personally rejoice that the country that has been nursing us is doing us the great service of forcing us to stand on our own feet. In the sentence I quoted a while ago, Mr. Kierans said:
The tremendous savings generated in the United States.
Why does not the Minister of Finance reconsider our monetary system, so that we too can generate the capital and the credit we need for the development and the progress of our economy?
I think that the present Minister of Finance, being a good accountant, would be able to father that new economy which would make enough capital available to enable us to develop ourselves a Canadian economy. As a matter of fact, we do not need foreigners to do this. We are able to do it ourselves.
Let me give you an example. Only recently, the sales tax on building materials was increased. In this connection, I read in today's papers that according to some municipal authorities, interest rates will rise and it will be harder to obtain capital on the American market, precisely because of this new tax.
Mr. Chairman, it is Canadian citizens who are responsible for the development of municipalities, because they are the ones who

manufacture and assemble the materials used in the construction of public buildings or of public services in Canada. In fact, there is only one thing which our Canadian citizens have not made up to now and that is cheques and coupons, the bits of paper which are used to carry out that development.

What is he doing at the present time? He is still trying to solve the problems resulting from the decisions of foreign capitalists. Yet, the solution is simple. As the hon. member was saying, credit accounts-

But the Minister of Finance should endeavour to realize that our country is able to develop itself and that it is not only on account of our lack of capital that it is not doing so, for capital can be more easily built up than our country.

This lesson should help us find a new orientation for our economic system.
These days, we are considering the establishment of an economic council. It is sought to develop our industries by means of an economic development council. Even if Canada has the required workers, industrialists and producers, it cannot put them to

work because it does not have the permission of a few financiers.
Under those conditions, and in view of the restrictions imposed by a handful of small American or foreign financiers, I wonder what a group of members of parliament who have been democratically elected by the people, can decide.
I am also wondering what is the meaning of democracy in our country. And what can the Canadian people say if all those decisions are subject to the approval of foreign financiers?
The Minister of Finance is no longer the minister of finance. He cannot control his finance because he is always the victim of decisions made by foreign financiers who control everything. A case in point, the moment he announces that a tax will be levied he has to withdraw it because a certain stock exchange president has come to see him.
Indeed, I should like to know why the Minister of Finance does not hasten to inform President Kennedy of all the administrative difficulties he himself had to face when he imposed his 30 per cent tax. He should even lose no time in sending Mr. Kierans to Washington to explain to them the administrative difficulties facing the Canadian government. I think President Kennedy would withdraw his tax since we are told it is for that very reason that our Minister of Finance had to withdraw his. But let me tell you that, for my part, I never believed that administrative difficulties had forced the Minister of Finance to withdraw his 30 per cent tax on the sale of Canadian shares to non-residents. In fact, I can give him examples of many other taxes which have given rise to more serious administrative difficulties, not only to the Minister of Finance, but to all Canadian taxpayers. In my opinion, if there is someone who should meet with difficulties, it should be the Minister of Finance and not the taxpayers.
Nonsense. Has not the sales tax on building materials given rise to administrative difficulties for those who are in the building field? One needs merely to look over the letters of protest sent to the minister to see that my contention is right.
In fact, have we ever heard in Canada of a single tax with which Canadian taxpayers had no difficulties? I challenge the Minister of Finance to name one tax that did not result in difficulties for Canadian taxpayers. Yet they were never withdrawn. Quite the contrary, they were increased as much as possible.

All levels of governments increase those taxes, and the Minister of Finance is anxious to make us believe he withdrew his 30 per cent tax because he was faced with administrative difficulties. Nonsense.
All taxes cause difficulties. The true reason is that the United States wanted to establish its own tax.
It is well known that the American under secretary of state exerted pressure. The Minister of Finance gave in and, less than a month later, the American government levied exactly the same tax, except that its rate is 15 per cent instead of 30 per cent, and that the profit goes to the American government instead of the Canadian government.
Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, I did not take the floor to protest against the 15 per cent tax proposed by President Kennedy. On the contrary, it has my full approval, and if the President of the United States wants to increase it to 75 per cent, so much the better. This tax will prove that we cannot rely on American capital, on American investment to ensure the growth of our economy and that if we want to survive in the world's economic struggle, we must act as the United States did when they wanted to develop their country, we must create our own capital.
As a matter of fact, they were successful in that field. They created the necessary capital to establish the whole industry they have at present, and they went even further. They created additional capital to develop Africa, South America, and other countries and to invest in Canada.
Would anyone try to make us believe that Canada is not able to do the same? If the Minister of Finance is prepared to accept a shortage of capital because the Americans want it that way, I am against it, I cannot accept the situation and I tell the Minister of Finance that he must assume his responsibilities, since it is his duty and he must set up a monetary system in order that Canadians be the masters of their capital and this not only as far as administration, but also as far as creation is concerned, because money, capital and credit are created some place; they do not fall like manna from heaven, they do not grow in potato fields, they are created some place.
Capital is created by men, by individuals. There has not always been a monetary system; it is a human invention. Men have invented

Mr. Chairman, I continue my remarks to say that, today, we have an example which shows us that at this time we must endeavour to reorganize our finances and our system in order that we may take action and develop by ourselves.
Since the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act are to be amended next year, I think a study and an analysis should be undertaken right away of the transformations and amendments which should be brought forward so

Income Tax Act
that the Minister of Finance, the government and the Bank of Canada can create in our country the capital needed for our own development, without having to toady or to grovel before foreign investors as we have been doing since confederation.
Mr. Chairman, it is urgent to develop a new school of thought in our country: the finance separatist school. We must separate from our continuous dependence on foreign investors, and such a project would be Canadian from sea to sea. The ten provinces could set up an arrangement to see to it that our country would become independent from foreign capital. It is simple, Mr. Chairman.
I ask the Minister of Finance to think it over. Let him pay a visit to his bank manager. Let him go and get a loan from him. We saw him lately pass a resolution to borrow $1,500 million, but let him ask his bank manager what he does when he grants a $100,000 loan to a friend. The bank manager will tell him that he takes his pen and writes some figures in a bank book. At that moment, he is creating new credit which will represent the wealth of the nation.
Why should we leave that in the hands of one individual only? Why should not the wealth of the country instead be represented by assets and credit which would belong to Canada and be under the "control" of the Bank of Canada instead of remaining under the "control" of a few investors? The Minister of Finance should consider the way the necessary credit for the development of Canada can be built up, and then, he will not complain, as he did today, about the American government levying a new tax that will slow down our country's business.
Is it not amazing, Mr. Chairman-and serious, in my opinion-that a mere statement by the president of another country is enough to bring about on the Canadian stock exchange fluctuations as the ones we have witnessed yesterday and today. A mere statement by the president of another country is enough. If we were really controlling our economy, we would not be the victims of those decisions made outside of Canada.
If the minister accepts this situation, we do not. We have to learn to become an adult nation, capable of governing ourselves without being continually in bondage to foreign governments and dependant on their decisions as far as our economy, our policy or social system are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, it is a lesson for us. Let us try to profit by it and to improve our legislation in order to become truly independent in our own country.

Mr. B rewin: Mr. Chairman, I should perhaps first state that I propose to discuss the income tax resolution. This may limit my rhetorical style, but that is the subject upon which I propose to address the committee.
I hope you will pardon the personal note when I say I rather regret that my first contribution to either the budget debate, or the discussion on the resolutions arising from it, does not take the form of being complimentary to the Minister of Finance and of commending the resolutions.
I would very much like to have done so for the personal reason of long friendship with the minister and a great admiration for his attractive qualities. Also I would like to have gained a reputation for originality, because I have not noticed anybody either in the house or in the committee saying a kind word to the minister or about his budget. But unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, the fact of the matter is that candor compels me to say this is an extremely bad resolution, and I propose to try to say why I think so.
The purpose of the resolution, as announced by the minister, is to advance Canadian control of our economy. That is indeed a very laudable objective; but it is my view, on looking at this actual resolution, that it will not only fail to fulfil that purpose but, on the contrary, the natural result of the effects of this particular resolution will be to do precisely the opposite and minimize the degree of control which Canadians will have over their economy. I shall later give my reasons for saying that.
In my view, and I summarize what I am going to say before I say it, the resolution is administratively inept. It will succeed in irritating foreign investors and completely frustrate the good intentions it is supposed to serve. This resolution is both delusive and deceptive to anyone who believes it is likely to increase Canadian control of the economy.
The minister announced that its purpose was to deal with the problem of non-resident ownership and control of Canadian industry. He gave us some of the figures in his budget speech, and pointed out that in 1959 57 per cent of the manufacturing industry in Canada, 75 per cent of the petroleum and natural gas industry, and 61 per cent of the other mining and smelting industry were controlled

by non-residents. The resolution we are discussing was designed to deal with this problem, and I can say that no one in this corner of the house, or in this party, is likely to quarrel with that purpose or disagree with it as an attempt.
We are all facing this problem of foreign ownership and control, but in my submission it is not enough to have good intentions. We have been told that the road to hell is paved with good intentions, and I suggest that the road to political disaster can also be paved with them.
Let us examine the particular resolution in question. It provides, as the minister has told us, a form of incentive or a benefit, by way of accelerated write-off of depreciation, for corporations which are described in the resolution as having a degree-and I ask the committee to mark these words-a degree of Canadian ownership and control.
These corporations with this degree of Canadian ownership and control are to receive the benefits of the incentive in this accelerated write-off, and in another section of the resolution, in the diminution of the withholding tax.
Let us examine what corporations with a degree of Canadian ownership and control will so benefit, and what will be the result. There are two groups. I leave out some of the unnecessary additional classifications, but basically there are two groups. One is a corporation of which not less than 25 per cent of its voting shares are beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, or one or more corporations controlled in Canada, or a combination thereof. In other words an incentive is to be given to corporations, which are owned by foreign investors, to divest themselves of 25 per cent of their stock, and presumably to sell that stock to Canadians so that they will qualify for this particular incentive. This is one way in which they will qualify for the incentive.
I am not going into any elaborate discussion of the matter, but I say it is a perversion of language to suggest that a 25 per cent ownership of a wholly owned American subsidiary amounts to any control whatsoever. I know in law no less controlling situation than to be a minority shareholder where you have unified majority ownership on the other side. You have no control whatsoever. The very best you can do is make a nuisance of yourself under certain limited circumstances by seeking to get the corporation wound up and its assets sold. You do not control action in any shape or form by this 25 per cent ownership.
But, Mr. Chairman, that is not the real difficulty here. The real difficulty is that this will work this way: It will give an incentive
Income Tax Act
to the American corporations to try to divest themselves of part of their share capital to a minority of Canadians, and it may in turn give an incentive to Canadian investors to invest in these minority interests in foreign controlled corporations. Again I emphasize I am talking largely of wholly owned American subsidiaries.
I am fully aware of the fact that 25 per cent of ownership may give a control in certain circumstances, where the remaining ownership is widely diffused, but with a wholly foreign owned subsidiary this 25 per cent amounts to nothing that would in any circumstances be called control.
What will be the result of this provision? It is that Canadian investment funds, that might be available for investment in truly Canadian corporations, and which would give some real measure of control, will be drawn into this phoney sort of control, namely into minority interest in a wholly-owned subsidiary of a foreign corporation.
There is only a very limited amount of Canadian capital available for investment and it has been estimated-I do not know how accurately-that to acquire a 25 per cent interest in these foreign owned investments in Canada would require $4 billion. Even if a small percentage of that $4 billion, available in Canadian savings for investment, is channelled into this minority control by reason of this incentive, by so much will Canadian control in its own equities and ownership be divested from Canadian owned and controlled companies, and Canadian control will be diminished, rather than advanced under the terms of this resolution. Indeed the situation is worse than that because the second part of this resolution envisions that not even a minority interest will necessarily be Canadian.
Under clause (B) of the resolution it is provided that a corporation is deemed to be by law, under this resolution, to be a corporation with a degree of Canadian control-and I presume the statute will follow the same terminology-if:
-the voting shares of the corporation were listed on a recognized stock exchange in Canada and it is established, in prescribed manner, that no one non-resident shareholder owned beneficially, together with any other person associated with him at any time in any period, more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation,
There is an element of Canadianism in the fact that the shares have to be listed on a recognized stock exchange in Canada. I presume that means, under the regulations that apply to recognized stock exchanges, a certain amount of shares would have to be offered on that exchange for purchase by Canadians. But it is perfectly possible, under

Income Tax Act
this regulation, that a corporation would qualify for these incentives when, say, 74 per cent of the shares were owned by a syndicate in New York and 26 per cent of the shares were spread around amongst foreign investors in Philadelphia, Boston and what have you. Yet if the terms of this resolution were carried into the legislation this would be deemed to be a corporation with a degree of Canadian ownership and control. It certainly will have very little Canadian ownership, and I venture to suggest it will have practically no Canadian control.
Therefore the clause, if it is used as the basis of granting the incentive the minister speaks of as being an effective incentive-and that is how he opened his remarks-that particular incentive will be given to someone on the basis of a supposed "degree of Canadian ownership and control" when there is in fact no control and very little ownership. I say it will utterly fail to achieve the supposed purposes of the minister and the supposed purposes of this particular resolution. In fact, it aids precisely the opposite development; that is, the abstraction of Canadian investment funds from availability for investment in the ownership of their own equities.
Mr. Chairman, I had intended to spend a little time reading from various quotations in the financial press-I do not always get the opportunity to cite them in support of my own arguments and theories. These quotations point out the administrative weaknesses and difficulties of this proposed resolution. They are many and varied. The assessment of beneficial ownership is an extraordinarily difficult task and the possibilities for corporate manipulation are infinite. The administrative difficulties of applying this regulation will be tremendous, as has been pointed out by qualified financial advisers in the press. I think that part has to be looked into very carefully.
Then you get strange phrases like this, "One qualifies"-I think these were the minister's words-"for these incentives if there is not a non-resident shareholder, together with any other person associated with him who owns more than 75 per cent of the voting stock". It is true, Mr. Chairman, that this is not the legislation and is only the resolution, but what does a phrase like "any other person associated with him" mean? It is the vaguest, loosest sort of language, impossible to administer, with no real meaning. The ability to conceal the fact that a person is associated with you is the simplest thing in the manipulations of the financial world at the present time, and I defy the minister or his advisers to

produce legislation that will make that part of the resolution administratively workable or intelligent at all.
I just want to add this, Mr. Chairman. In my view the whole philosophy that underlies this resolution is punitive. When saying that, I think I speak for the party I represent in this house. The whole philosophy is one of punishment; it is punitive; it is gimmicky; it is not really tackling the problem that is involved. As I say, it will have the effect of irritating foreign investors who, as the minister says, we still need for the development of this country. But it will do nothing whatever to meet the real need, which is to promote and give leadership to the investment of Canadian funds in Canada, to mobilize Canadian resources for the development of our own country. The positive, and not the punitive, approach is the one that is necessary if this problem of foreign control is to be solved. Let us give up these punitive gimmicks of which this resolution is a sample and, I would say, a very poorly drawn and inadequate sample.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, in other circumstances I would have liked to conclude my remarks by urging the minister to withdraw this particular resolution. But I realize that unfortunately from his point of view the room for retreat and manoeuvre is limited at this stage; therefore I can hardly hope to persuade him to withdraw this resolution. But whether it is withdrawn or not, I say to him and to this committee that the excellent, well intentioned purposes which were announced for this particular resolution will not be served by the resolution and the legislation proposed, and that in actual fact it will defeat, rather than assist, the solution of the problem with which we are all concerned; that is, the problem of domestic, Canadian control of our own economic destiny.

interest is, in most cases, appropriate to ensure that a Canadian point of view is always available when company policy decisions are arrived at.

I think I will just leave it by saying that I was not completely convinced by all his arguments.

Mr. Chairman, this first paragraph deals with two different facets. It deals, in the first place, with an accelerated depreciation, which is one matter on which one could have a discussion and a debate and there might be differences of opinion as to the effect and the benefits derived therefrom. But I would suggest that this is perhaps the minor facet at the moment, despite what the minister said this morning about its importance. I think perhaps this is a minor part of the resolution, because when you adopt this resolution you are also adopting the definition of the Canadians of this corporation who, under certain circumstances, will be entitled to this accelerated depreciation.
I could not agree more with what was said a moment ago by the hon. member for Greenwood with regard to this matter. I agree entirely. It is a rather welcome relief that I do so because we cannot agree entirely on some of these matters. So far as the inadequacy of the definition, its purpose and its futility is concerned, that is something which goes to the root of the resolution. It is the reason why we should not allow the resolution to go through at this stage. The incentive or the depreciation in itself is not so important. It plays a part, of course; but once you adopt this paragraph you are adopt-
Income Tax Act
ing the same definition so far as the withholding tax is concerned, and when you are dealing with the withholding tax you are dealing with what I think is a particularly vicious and wicked section of the resolutions which should not be considered at any time.
What we are really doing here, as I see it-and if I am wrong I am sure the minister will correct me-is defining the good boys and the bad boys. The good boys are going to get cookies and cake by way of incentives; the bad boys are going to get hit over the head. I suggest that this is the first time in the western world which I can recall where there have been incentives for the good and not the bad, where there have been carrots and clubs for a given taxation period.
If I read the definition aright, the minister was faced with a very difficult administrative problem. There is no question about that; he admitted it. When he first brought in his bill he provided for 25 per cent Canadian ownership, although I think he faced the fact that this was probably impossible to administer. Anyway, he withdrew it and now you have a situation where a company must be listed on the Canadian stock exchange and not more than 75 per cent of such company can be owned by an individual or by associated companies. In other words, a small group. Let us take Ford of Canada, for example. If 74.89 per cent of Ford of Canada is controlled by the Ford family, shall we say, the other 25 per cent listed on the Canadian stock exchange could be-and in some other corporations they might be- owned by people in Ghana, in Holland, in Germany, in France, in Switzerland and in England, and not one single share owned in Canada. As long as the Canadian directors who are officials of the company are resident here and it is called a Canadian corporation, we are going to give it tax incentives and benefits. Let us take another example. My hon. friend for Ontario has a corporation in his constituency, General Motors, which employs a few dozen Canadians-14,000. General Motors, as I understand it, is a wholly-owned United States subsidiary. Whether that is right or wrong is a matter one could debate for some time. But we were told by the government that the fundamental problem was that of employment, of ensuring employment. I think a man who could get a job with General Motors would be just as happy as if he had got a job with Ford of Canada. Yet General Motors cannot qualify for these incentives, if they want to put in new equipment, because they are not in that category where they have a few resident

Income Tax Act
Canadian directors. They are the bad boys, whereas some other corporation would be a good boy.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that undoubtedly if there are shares listed on the Canadian market there is bound to be the odd Canadian investor. Surely this was not the intention of the minister when he wrote his first book. Surely this was not the intention of the minister when he wrote his second book. And surely this was not the intention of the minister when he wrote his budget. Then we were going to have at least 25 per cent Canadian control. How utilitarian that would be is debatable, yet it was a major objective and something which, if it could have been administered, might have been a success. But that has gone, and now you have left the 75 per cent ownership. As long as it is not more than 75 per cent owned outside Canada by associated companies or a family or group of that kind, then the other 25 per cent may be owned by Canadians in whole or in part, or may not be owned by Canadians at all. As long as you have the requisite number of Canadian directors who may now be officials of the company, which was precluded before-they may not even be Canadian citizens, but as long as they are Canadian residents-this qualifies the company for preferred treatment. As I have said, I do not think this is so vitally important in this case where we are dealing with depreciation, although that in itself is important. But it is of vital importance when we are going to deal with the withholding tax. Once we adopt the definition in this section, the position will be the same as when we are dealing with the withholding tax.
For that reason, particularly in view of what happened yesterday in the United States when we did not know, as the minister said, what the reactions would be or what results would flow from the presidential message, this is not the time to be adopting definitions or passing laws which will further complicate our relations with our investors in other countries. I would urge that the committee not pass this paragraph this afternoon but that it be stood over until such time as the situation is clarified. We think that the committee, the house and the country should have more opportunity to consider it and then deal with it concretely.
There are many other things which one could deal with, Mr. Chairman. I have a dozen questions which can be asked but I am sure others have too. All I want to do for the moment, in support of the hon. member for Greenwood, is to point out what

to my mind is the absolute futility and inconsistency of this definition. If there was ever a case of gimmickry on gimmickry, then this is a gimmick to outdo all the gimmicks in creation.

Mr. Chairman, as we are now discussing paragraph 1 of version 2 of the fourth edition of the budget I feel we must have some sympathy with the hon. member for Greenwood. I also have some sympathy with the Minister of Finance in the position he finds himself as minister. We all recognize the need for revenue, and one point which is so often missed by those who would comment on the federal financial scene is that the Minister of Finance has control over but one third of the expenditures which are within the four corners of our federal budget expenditure, because there are so many statutory items over which he has no real control. One can recognize that in this day and age the Minister of Finance requires extra revenues, in addition to which, of course, not only has he to meet the level of expenditure which existed prior to his assumption of office, but we have been given notice of a veritable flood of expenditures which are to come. Of these a good number will be statutory items or of a nature over which the minister will have no future control. So he has his problems.
The budget, the minister told us on opening night, was to be a budget which would stimulate industry and provide employment. Then on the famous Monday night when we had the explanations we were told that the purpose of the budget was to provide more revenue. Then, of course, we know that there was another objective in this budget, and this was the implementation of the philosophy of Canadianization of companies or Canadianiza-tion of foreign investment in Canada. But what has been the result? I would suggest to the minister this will have the contrary effect. We were told, with respect to the removal of the 30 per cent takeover tax, that this was being done because of administrative difficulties. I can understand the views of the minister in this regard and disagree heartily with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Lapointe whose knowledge in this field is, I suggest, in inverse proportion to his volubility when he talks about there being an absence of administrative difficulty. I have heard it said in Ottawa-it is notorious-that the people in the Department of National Revenue responsible for these matters were consulted somewhat late in the day and that the difficulties were therefore not apparent until the minister was committed to the budget and had announced

his plans. Then he was obliged to say: we planned to do this but we now find it is impossible.
This provision was, we were told, an attempt to get United States investment out of equities and into bond holdings. I have no quarrel with the proposal made by the United States President. He and his government are facing a serious and complicated problem. They are taking action and it will affect us. But the effects of this proposal, if the proposal is implemented will, I suggest to the hon. gentleman, be the reverse of what he wished to accomplish by means of his budget. The heaviest incidence of the proposed United States tax will be on longer term investments and bond holdings. Instead of United States money coming into Canada and flowing into the bond market rather than into equities, the reverse is likely to happen because the United States proposal would subject investments in bond holdings to the heavier tax rate. Admittedly this is what appears on the surface of the president's proposal, and we do not know how the measure may be amended by congress. However, this is what I gather from the face of it and I intend to leave the matter at that point.
Now we come to the purpose of these resolutions, which is to provide an incentive for certain categories of companies which have a so-called Canadian content. They are told that at least 25 per cent of their directors should be resident in Canada in order to qualify for these benefits or, as was explained by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, there must be some odd combination in relation to the holding of voting shares. On this point, the resolution is far from clear. It says-"And it is established in prescribed manner". I realize, of course, that we cannot expect to have the details with regard to this at the resolution stage but it would be most interesting to know what the prescribed manner will be to establish that-
-no one non-resident shareholder owned beneficially, together with any other person associated with him at any time in the period, more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation.
Then we come to this business of the number of directors. No doubt it is felt that by this provision a certain Canadian content would be given to a corporation or business. I do not know what type of corporation the minister has been accustomed to deal with, but I can tell him that there are a number of jurisdictions in this country where it is possible to establish corporations in which the directors need hold no shares at all. It is possible to do that today in the province of Alberta; it merely means the inclusion of an appropriate clause in the articles of association. I myself, as a solicitor, have often par-28902-5-154
