ticipated in such arrangements merely to comply with certain provisions and regulations of this particular kind. I would strongly suggest to the minister that this requirement is a hollow one. It means nothing. There could be compliance with the letter but not with the spirit of the law. Companies can get away with it, and it means absolutely nothing.
I am puzzled, too, by the procedures to be used to determine the ownership of shares where the Canadian resident holds shares in a mutual fund. When these funds are then put into equity shares in a Canadian corporation how do we arrive at a true appreciation of the share holding? We are getting down to certain situations where there will have to be knife edge decisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not under this provision.

Well, I should like the minister to consider this. There may be an appropriate answer, but where one has this 25 per cent Canadianism, or anywhere where there is a percentage requirement of shareholders, what does one do where there are holdings in a mutual fund?
There is another point. I suggest the requirement that a certain number of directors should be residents of Canada can be readily defeated as far as Canadianization is concerned. There are hundreds of companies in Alberta, for instance, which are involved in oil field supplies and in the oil business. Their directors are, for a good part, United States citizens, residents of this country who are shuttled back and forth by their parent corporations in the United States. These men may live for two, three, or five years in Canada, but they are here to carry on the business of a subsidary company according to the dictates of head office policy, which is American. They have done a tremendous job for the industry, but I say to the minister that as far as introducing an element of Canadianization into these companies is concerned, the requirement in these regulations means nothing. It will not introduce that element. If the government intends to introduce Canadianization in this way, let these men be domiciled in Canada or I should say become citizens of Canada. I admit it will be much more restrictive, but it is a restriction to achieve a particular purpose or advantage with respect to investment in new equipment and new plant. It is a restrictive rule, so if it is the intention of the government to give an advantage to the Canadian element why not provide that it shall be a Canadian citizen who shall be a director?
There is one further point on which I would quarrel with this resolution. I do not think that the allowance of up to 50 per cent

Income Tax Act
ior depreciation in a year, particularly in new business, means anything except in the odd case. If you are establishing a new business you must look to the long pull. You are not necessarily going to make money in the first two years of business. It is only the rare bird who is able to operate in the black in the first two years. Yet this individual or company is being given the advantage of a write-off of up to 50 per cent for depreciation in those two years. What good is it to him if he is already in a loss position? The purpose of this depreciation incentive is so that he will have less taxes to pay and more money available for further investment or to recover for himself.
I also suggest to the minister that even if he did avail himself of the 50 per cent, or whatever lesser percentage he chose to take, all he would be doing would be to hasten the evil day when he would have no further allowable write-off. Therefore in the third year, or whatever subsequent year it may be, he will then be bearing the full impact of the tax on income which has been established at a certain figure because there is no more depreciation allowance. You cannot escape it. You are not giving 150 per cent depreciation in this instance; you are limiting yourself to 100 per cent. Whether you write it off in two years, four years or ten years you are still going to be limited to the cost that you are going to depreciate. It is true that you are advancing it now, but three years hence you are going to be hit with the whole burden.
There are other things I should like to say with respect to other paragraphs in the resolution, particularly as to related companies. I think that is a pernicious provision. I have fought against it and there are others present who know how I have fought against it. I think it is induced by a rather illogical division between small businesses and large businesses and I hope the minister will look at it because I think there is room here for manoeuver. There is room to do something constructive with regard to corporate income tax. I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, that this provision has too many hooks and unknown dangers for us to pass it immediately, and I would prefer to see this item stand so that we can go on with others that are less controversial.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that is a good suggestion. I would suggest that we leave the discussion of this particular paragraph, not the resolution, move on to other paragraphs and then come back to it. I thought that the main point made by the hon.

member for Edmonton West was in connection with the depreciation or capital cost allowance of 50 per cent. It seemed to me that he was thinking primarily of new businesses; at least, that is what he talked about. With great respect to him, I would think that this provision would prove to be a tremendous incentive to many established businesses to expand. It has been in the past when people have been offered accelerated depreciation. It proved to be very effective, and I have no doubt in my mind that this will prove to be a very great incentive to increased capital investment in the private sector of the economy. But I agree with the hon. member that this will apply perhaps especially to established companies rather than to those that are not yet established.
I do not think I have anything more to say except that I agree with the suggestion that it might be a good idea if we went on with some of the other paragraphs and came back to No. 1 later.

I have some questions I should like to ask the minister in connection with the depreciation allowance. Would it not be possible for a person to acquire a debt as well as a depreciable piece of machinery costing several hundred thousand dollars? In other words, the piece of machinery might not be needed now but rather six, eight or ten years from now and in order to take advantage of this provision the company would buy a piece of equipment for installation at some later date. The depreciation allowance would be granted, even though the company had made the purchase on the time payment plan with only a small down payment.
I have one or two other points. I was interested in the remarks of the minister about the incentive for expansion. He did not refer to expansion to meet certain markets in his remarks. I am wondering whether or not we are trying to entice people to expand their plant where markets do not exist. In my business experience, when the market was there the money generally was readily available to go ahead and expand. I am wondering, however, about creating an incentive just for the sake of expansion without knowing whether or not there is going to be a market for the product, be it a machine or something else, that is going to be made. Would the minister care to comment on these points?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to the first point, Mr. Chairman, it would be possible, of course, for a business to buy a piece of machinery for $300,000, or whatever the figure was that the hon. member suggested, that it would not need for some years and claim this depreciation. However, I cannot imagine many companies doing that because, after all, they would get

certain tax advantages, but only up to 50 per cent and not many people will invest in machinery and have to spend at least half their own money for that purpose unless they are going to use it. There might be the odd case but I suspect only on the part of some company that had so much money that it did not know what to do with it.
On the second point, I quite agree that most businessmen are not likely to expand their operations unless they are satisfied that markets are available. But I think we all know that in Canada we have many businesses that have not kept themselves as modern and up to date as they perhaps would like to have done. I think we know that there is a great deal of obsolescent machinery in Canada and that the prime need in this country is to make our businesses efficient and modern in every sense of the word so that they can face up to the kind of competition with which they are now confronted. The purpose of the incentive is to encourage companies to modernize, to scrap obsolescent machinery and to replace it with the most modern machinery it can acquire.

I should like to have the minister relate what he has said to the remarks of the Minister of Defence Production the other day when he said we must temper our efficiency with the idea of providing jobs. It seems to me there is a direct conflict here. In essence, we are saying we must modernize, get more up to date machinery, which will bring about automation to a greater degree, provide a greater degree of efficiency and a better product; yet the Minister of Defence Production, if you will refer to his speech in Hansard, said we must temper our efficiency, our automation, with the idea of providing more jobs. I should like to see if the minister can relate the two objectives because there seems to be a conflict.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I was not in the house when the Minister of Defence Production made the remark to which my hon. friend refers.
You will find the remarks there, all right.

I will have to look them up. I am pretty sure the Minister of Defence Production would agree with me, however, when I say that in general terms, and certainly there may be some exceptions, if Canada is to prosper, if we are going to compete with other countries as we must, we shall have to do everything we can to modernize our industry in this country. I do not think there can be much quarrel with that. The hon. member used the word "temper", and 28902-5-1545

there may be occasions where other considerations have to be taken into account for a while, but by and large if we do not keep up to date in this country then we are going to get into a great deal of difficulty.
I agree with you, and I disagree with the Minister of Defence Production.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to divide my remarks into three parts this afternoon. I understand we are still dealing with paragraph 1. In particular, I should like to say a few words in a general way as a member of the House of Commons, a person who lives in the city of Calgary and represents the riding of Bow River which contains about one third of the people in the city of Calgary. I believe that in the city of Calgary, on a per capita basis, we have more people from the United States than we have from any other part of Canada. We have, in a city of 235,000, at least 35,000 or 40,000 people from the United States.
In fact, recently I was talking with the United States consul there, Mr. Madill, who has just been moved from the city of Calgary to New Zealand. He says it is one of the busiest consulate offices in the whole of Canada. I refer to those facts because I should like to mention certain things which took place during the campaign. I do not want to flog a dead horse, because the campaign is over, but these events set the whole tone of the resolution, the whole tone of the budget. If we look back at the campaign for a moment we find, and I say this without any equivocation, that far more irresponsible than any taxes that may have been imposed or attempted to be imposed by the former government, was the budget. Yet, when we tried to develop a plan, when we encouraged Canadians to invest more money in their own business, we were then labelled antiAmerican.
I am going to go further. I did not intend to go that far this afternoon, but there was a most vicious attack made because they labelled us anti-American. They labelled the leader of our party anti-American. I say that I do not blame the newspapers in the United States for writing that kind of propaganda: I blame the people now sitting on the treasury benches. I believe the kind of publicity that Canada is getting is probably the result of that situation that developed. The people of the United States generally are beginning to realize that probably their true friends after all were the members of the Conservative government and not the present Liberal government. I think we should always remember, and I think we should remember it outside of the house particularly, that when

Income Tax Act
you attack the Prime Minister of your country, then you are attacking your country as a whole. This is something that was accomplished by those people who now sit on the treasury benches.
As I have said, I come from the city of Calgary which does contain many people from the United States. I am going to be personal for a moment. I am married to a person who is a fifth generation American. During the campaign, because we were pro-Canadian, propaganda was poured out to the effect that we were anti-American. This was false; it was deceitful; it was wrong, and it was irresponsible to the country.
I was interested in the minister's last remark before he sat down concerning competition, and how Canada must compete with other countries industrially. One of the problems of competing is, of course, modernizing our plants. One of the phrases we have heard quite often lately is to get the economy rolling in order to increase productivity. I have said over and over again when I have spoken on this side of the house, and when I sat on the other side during the time the Conservatives were in office, that we should honestly try to reduce taxes.
I believe, in that regard, I should put an interesting story on the record. We are always bringing forward programs or attempting to bring forward programs, it seems, in order to win votes. These programs increase the taxes and take taxes from private industry and from the wage earner and, as a result, increase the cost of production. Then, we are not able to compete with some of the other countries, particularly the communist countries who say their economic penetration into the western world is greater than any other kind of penetration.
I should like to put this story on record with regard to taxes before I speak to the resolution. It is a story that is reported in "Vital Speeches of the Day", for March, 1963, at page 346. This is the report of a speech on "Our Most Precious Possession", by Mr. Doan. This is what he said:
There is a story of an old Indian who owned some oil land. He sold it for quite a sizeable sum of money. Soon thereafter the internal revenue service sent a man to see him for he had never filed a tax return. He asked why he should give 25 per cent of this money he had received to the government. The tax agent patiently explained that the government did a lot for him. It protected him from his enemies, it cared for him when he was sick, it gave him dams which made huge lakes for him to fish, and power for lights for his hut, and free money when he grew old, and for these purposes it needed money.
This is the reply the Indian gave to the man from the internal revenue department:
Yes, I understand. It is like this: I have a dog and the dog is hungry. He comes to me and begs
[Mr. Woolliams.l
food. I say to him, "My dear faithful dog, I see you are very hungry. X am sorry for you. I shall give you meat." I then take my knife, cut off the dog's tail, give it to him, and say, "Here, my faithful dog, be nourished by this nice piece of meat."
This is exactly the kind of tax system we have in this country. This is exactly what we are trying to do so far as the tax structure of this country is concerned.
I should like to spend just a few moments in referring to the new tax that has been implemented by the United States. I should like to quote something which appeared in this morning's Gazette, July 19. I quote from the article.
Eric W. Kierans, president of the Montreal and Canadian stock exchanges, noted that "Canadians have always relied on the large pools of savings generated in the United States to finance a higher rate of growth in Canada, at cheaper cost, than would have been possible otherwise."
With Canadians cut off from a ready access to American markets, "higher interest rates seem inevitable."
It goes on to say:
As a result, we can expect a slowing down of economic activity at a time when we already have high unemployment.
I do not think anyone would suggest that that tax was implemented because of what has taken place in what I classify as an irresponsible budget, but I do say that Canada should have been left out of the list of 22 nations mentioned, or at least our Minister of Finance should be in a position to negotiate on behalf of Canada. But, when one looks at the terms of the budget and at what he tried to do in it, but which he withdrew and retreated from like Napoleon, one cannot except the Minister of Finance to say, "Go easy with us. We are Canadians. We do not want that kind of tax. It is going to hurt our economy, and it is going to mean maybe another	100,000 men unemployed next
winter."
We cannot negotiate in that fashion because we have put our worst foot forward and the chickens have come home to roost; and this was done by people who said we were antiAmerican and they were pro-Canadian.
An increase in interest rates could easily develop. I am not a student of this, but I question whether the minister has really completely conceived of the situation between Canada and the United States economically, and what this might mean to our exchange problems. We may face tighter money, and tight money brings back many problems and will increase the number of our unemployed.
The whole background of the budget, and the whole principle behind the books written in the past by the minister, was that if we

followed certain steps, laid down in the budget, it would mean full employment for Canadians, whatever that means-when you have less than 4 per cent unemployed. Then of course you have full employment, according to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing would make me happier than to have all the people in the constituency of the hon. member for Lapointe in the position where they had lots of jobs to choose from. I am sure he would agree that would be just fine.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that, because I do not think any member of parliament presently sitting in the house, or any former member, has said he did not want full employment. Every government that sat over there has striven for the same thing. After all, governments may make mistakes innocently and logically, but every government that sat on that side worked for full employment.
However the point I want to make is that when there was unemployment in 1957, when the Conservatives were in office, to listen to hon. gentlemen opposite one would think we had invented something new in the political world.
Coming directly to paragraph 1 of the resolution, I am inclined to agree with our financial critic that what is so strange about the resolution is that it puts one group of people in one pen and another group in another pen. You have the bad boys in one pen and the good boys in another, and one of the difficulties is to differentiate between the good and the bad by reading the resolution itself because, when you approve of the first part of the resolution, as other hon. members have said, you have then approved of the definition of what you mean by a good boy and what you mean by a bad boy.
But even if one were to take that part out and looked at the resolution as it reads in reference to the 50 per cent depreciation, what does this really mean? Applying it to new companies going into areas where there are surplus labour pools, and there is one in my own riding, Drumheller, most of these companies which start out, buy new machines and new processing equipment and would not show a profit for a number of years; so that actually the resolution as it stands is really superfluous. It really does not mean anything even if applied to companies now in operation that are showing a good profit, because if you write the depreciation off for the first two or three years then it is gone and they are going to pay this taxation on profits in later years.
The minister has already changed one of the provisions of the budget, cutting the 11 per cent sales tax back to 4 per cent and amortizing it over a period of years, but this

Income Tax Act
is going to be dangerous and the full tax will be paid in a number of years.
With reference to the definition of what is a Canadian corporation and what is not, it seems to me we could have a situation, as pointed out by the financial critic of our party, where Canadians would not own any part of a company but it still could be categorized as a Canadian company. Where does that put us? It merely discriminates as between one company and another. Of two companies having almost the same identical structure, one may comply with this provision and the other may not. A definition of that nature is very dangerous and it is certainly a new type of thinking in discriminating in favour of one company as against another.
If it applies to the Ford Company and not to General Motors then it is unfairly discriminatory and unjust. On that ground I support my fellow colleagues in their contention that the resolution should be stood; but I go further and say not only should it be stood but it should be withdrawn, as the minister did with other portions of the budget, in his retreat like Napoleon from Moscow.
I want to clear up just one point. Would the minister give a definition of residence?

Does it mean the residence of domicile, or does it mean ordinary residence? How long must the residence be, for instance, in Canada? Also, if the minister can give us a definition of "resident"-and I am sure he can-would he give statistics to-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that there is nothing in the Income Tax Act, or very little, defining "resident" but that it is to be found in the common law of the country. That is why, not being a lawyer, I am not prepared to give a snap decision; I do not think I am qualified to do it.

Then without the definition at all, and referring to the common law of Canada, has the minister any figures to show the number of non-Canadians resident in Canada who are at the present time directors of a corporation subsidiary wholly owned other than in Canada? I am asking the minister this question because there must have

been a reason for putting this residence qualification into the resolution. First of all, apparently the question has not crossed the minister's mind as to what is the definition of a resident of Canada for the purposes of this measure. Second, in putting this qualification into the resolution he must have had some object in view. There have been a great many "airy fairy" decisions on the budget already, and if this is going to be carried into this budget resolution, surely it should be stood over right now until such time as this normal type of question can be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have in mind "resident" in the general understanding of the word, but I am not in a position to give the hon. member a legal definition of it. My hon. friend may be a lawyer-he probably is-and if so, his knowledge of the common law would be very valuable to the committee, I am sure. I was not quite clear about the hon. member's second question with regard to the number of directors of various Canadian companies. There are no statistics at all on that.

The question is this. The minister must have had something in view when he started talking about residence as being a qualification for a director of a corporation which was wholly owned in the United States, or a subsidiary. Has he any idea as to how many non-Canadians would fit into this category at the present time, because if they are resident in Canada, according to the common law or any other definition set up by the regulations which will come into effect with the passing of these resolutions, surely that fact would qualify them under this paragraph and they could be non-Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
In fact, they would be in no different category than prior to the passing of this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This resolution contemplates that directors will qualify if they are ordinarily living in Canada and therefore familiar with Canadian points of view.
Then there could well be figures in the department at the present time which would indicate how many non-Canadians who are resident here are directors of corporations wholly owned outside Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to have to tell the hon. member that there are no such statistics.
(Translation):
Just like France.

Indeed, I could point out to the President of the Privy Council that, according to today's newspapers, during the first half of 1963, Americans bought $590 million worth of Canadian bonds, that is 67 per cent of the over-all amount of foreign bonds purchased by United States citizens. Mr. Chairman, Canada, which sold nearly 67 per cent of all foreign securities bought by the United States during the first six months of 1963, will be the first country affected by President Kennedy's plan. I feel it is our government's duty to suggest to the United States a preferential treatment for Canada, based on a good neighbour policy.
After the hullabaloo of Hyannis Port, and in spite of the outcry directed against the previous government during the last election campaign, the present government has done nothing, and Canadians feel disappointed.
The Minister of Finance urges us not to exercise ourselves unduly, as the proposed legislation has yet to be approved by the United States congress, and this may take several months. We are told that even if the measure were passed in the fall, it might find itself seriously amended.

Income Tax Act
The Minister of Finance thus tries to bring us some comfort, but actually we are left dangling in mid-air. Our financial circles find it much worse to remain in such state of uncertainty, than to know hard facts.
Mr. Chairman, it does seem rather childish to try and seek solace in the thought that the legislation has not yet been approved by congress, for we know, through the president's statement, that the proposed measure would become retroactive as from yesterday July 18, and we are aware that the Canadian stock exchanges have already been affected by the United States proposal.
Besides, one has merely to study the stock exchange to appreciate the effect of the new measure taken by the United States on the Canadian market.
Mr. Chairman, bearing in mind the action taken by the United States against Canada, we should consider very carefully the resolutions under study.
I believe also that the warnings given by the members for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) and for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), should be taken into serious consideration by the house before taking actions that would be merely aggravating, inefficient and would cause uneasiness in Canada itself. These measures, instead of stirring up industry and trade, will result in a more serious decline in business.
Mr. Chairman, we must be very careful when we are dealing with our neighbours to the south. We can see the extent to which what is going on south of the 45th parallel can affect our economy. That is why I believe that, if the Minister of Finance wants to promote Canadian economy, he must find perfectly accurate means which leave no room for doubt, in order that there be no discrimination between investors residing in Canada and those who invest money in Canada, that is foreign investors and Canadian investors. There should be no discrimination between them.
A climate of prosperity must be restored in Canada. We should welcome foreign capital to a certain extent, and that is what must be determined with the greatest care.
Let us not forget that, in all Canadian cities, from the smallest to the largest, municipal councils are spending vast sums of money to bring in new industries. I might point out
[Mr. Balcer.l
that it makes very little difference to those municipal councils whether the funds are American, French, English or Canadian. What they want is work for the Canadian people.
I realize we could go too far in that direction, but nevertheless we must make sure that all steps taken to curb foreign investments are capable of having beneficial results and do not constitute an obstacle to the development of our country.
That is why I feel those resolutions, as drafted, do not suit that purpose and why I agree with the views expressed by the hon. members I have mentioned at the beginning of my remarks.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, after quite a number of people have spoken on these resolutions it might be rather difficult to sound original, but perhaps something is to be said for expressing a somewhat similar idea in a different way; and sometimes the purposes of emphasis might be served by repetition by a number of people. On the question of emphasis, for example, it is not too often that I have heard in this house speeches made by hon. members on the left hand side of these benches quoted with approval. However, I did think that the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood touched upon what I consider to be one of the most fundamental faults in the budget presented by this government, namely the concept of the punitive aspect of taxation as compared to the encouragement of Canadians to achieve what the government is setting out to do. Certainly nothing could be more unsettling to the country as a whole, or more discouraging to investors both here and abroad, that the wild gyrations of the minister in withdrawing so many of the budget items. But it was not just the fact that these items had to be changed which was so bad; it was the fact that they were so startling and severe. The takeover tax, which was so quickly withdrawn, in itself could have done very little harm in a very short time if it had not been such a rude departure from all that had been expected of this government. While nothing may be gained, in some instances, from refighting the last election, I think that in order to appreciate the impact which this action had on the country, the effect it has had on the budget, and how it is affecting the confidence of investors and businessmen in this country, we should look again at the situation.
The fact is that the Conservatives had been branded as anti-American. They had been branded as anti-American by the concerted

efforts of Liberal propaganda over a considerable period of time. I would say that for political purposes the Liberals had gone far out on a limb on this and had played the theme that they are the friends of the Americans, and had stressed the importance of having a government friendly to the United States. They had sold the country on that, and sold the Americans to quite an extent on the idea that they would be that government. They had sold the people of this country on this, that if they came into power their mere assumption of office would restore the confidence of the business community. Here would be a government which would get along well with the United States, and in this way it would restore the confidence of the United States investors and Canadian investors and smooth the path toward economic well-being.
It is against this background that we must consider the action of the government. In addition to the budget as originally presented there were the items which have now been removed from it, and the budget resolutions are before us now; all are inextricably woven together. Certainly I thought there was some justification for the early Liberal propaganda when the change of government first came about, and that there might be something to the fact that the business community now had more confidence in the government than they had when the Conservatives were there. Certainly, all the organs of propaganda, the press in this country most of which had been favourable to the Liberals, as well as most of the press in the United States immediately began to hammer home the theme that now we had a government which understood cooperation, a government which was steady and reliable, a government which would take the commonsense viewpoint which this country needed if it was to meet the challenge ahead. I think the tide of propaganda which poured out did, for a little while begin to have an effect. Businessmen began to feel that at least the situation had stabilized, that we had a government which could swing the country behind it and that we would enjoy a period of stability, if nothing else. When we measure these expectations against the dismay brought about by the punitive measures announced by the Minister of Finance, we begin to understand the degree of shock felt by our friends in the United States who had hoped for so much. Had such a measure been introduced by a Conservative government which, through constant propaganda, had been branded as anti-American, it might have been considered in a different light. It might have been resented to a certain extent, and those who had been influenced by propaganda might have tried to make something
Income Tax Act
more out of it; but I believe it would have been considered fairly objectively. However, it was presented by a government which had done nothing but stress the importance of friendship with the United States, a government which had made so much political capital out of our balance of payments difficulties. When we appreciate this fully, we begin to realize why there was so much consternation at the hon. gentleman's announcement, not only in this country but throughout the United States.
We in this house have begun to recover in the last day or two from the shock we felt at President Kennedy's message to congress about the contemplated tax on shareholdings abroad. It should be remembered that the position of the United States in this regard is very different from our own. Canada is almost completely dependant on outside capital for its continued economic expansion. President Kennedy could implement a step such as this knowing that its results, while they might annoy foreign institutions, would not affect him too adversely, because United States generates more than sufficient capital within its own borders for its own needs. For anyone to suggest that if President Kennedy can do it a nation such as ours can do it, is to miss the point completely. Canada is just emerging from its position as a supplier of raw materials. We are only beginning to find our real stature as a manufacturing nation and we have a long way to go before we achieve the industrial capacity we must have if wTe are to overcome our employment difficulties. There is no suggestion that in the near future we are likely to become independent of outside sources of capital for investment. For a long time we shall need substantial sums to build up the industrial complex for which we must strive.
Since we are today so extremely dependant, we are therefore extra sensitive to the reactions of our friends, not just to friends in the United States but to those of potential investors around the world. This is what makes the budget resolutions so important. It is this extreme sensitivity which has led to so much consternation throughout this country. It is this extreme sensitivity, this extreme reliance on the confidence of other investors, which I suggest must make us extra cautious and extra critical with regard to the remaining budget resolutions. To begin with, we must see if there is in the remainder of these resolutions the same sort of punitive attitude which has been taken with regard to almost every item so far. I am suggesting we should look at each item on the basis of asking ourselves whether we find an attempt to drive people into doing what we want them to do, to punish them if they do not react in what we consider to be

Income Tax Act
the proper way, or whether we find an honest attempt to encourage them to invest their money in ways which will best help this nation. If we do this we will be looking at the resolutions in a manner which is most likely to help both the government and the country.
I am not at all encouraged by what I see on a quick review of these resolutions. I am not happy with the provisions made for judging what is Canadian ownership. To begin with, it seems to me we find here a preoccupation with surface appearances rather than with what really happens down deep. In fact, mere window dressing and bookkeeping effects are, I suggest, what we have here. Certainly, anyone who is at all conversant with Canadian affairs is aware of the necessity to overcome our balance of payments difficulties. These difficulties are, I suggest, tied to the fact that we are so dependant on outside capital. Canada, as I said, a minute ago, is only now emerging as a manufacturing nation but Canadians are not heavy investors. It does seem to me that where one has a country which is so much in need of capital for its development and where the inhabitants are perhaps the most cautious investors per capita of any in the world, what we should most look for in budget resolutions is a way in which we can change Canadians into investors rather than savers.
It does not make sense to punish some people for transferring shares-to discriminate between one class of shareholders and another by means which, I suggest, are artificial, particularly at a time when we are overlooking at least one most obvious source of capital. There is nothing in these budget resolutions, I suggest, designed to encourage Canadians to invest more. There is nothing in them designed to encourage Canadian companies to get Canadians to buy more of their shares. I suggest it would be hard to tag a scheme as being mere bookkeeping or more propaganda if there were solid tax incentives allowed to a company which could say that a larger percentage of its shares was actually held by Canadians. We should not look only to the Canadian financial community or to the major trust companies for funds. It does not take a lot of arithmetic to consider that we have four or five million working people in this country and if we could encourage each of them to invest $100 in Canadian companies we would almost halve our balance of payment difficulties.
It may be I am too pessimistic when I suggest $100 per year, or maybe I am too optimistic. I am suggesting that this would provide a large untapped pool and that in the budget resolutions there is not the slightest attempt to get at it. I am aware that the Liberals during the election campaign had

a scheme to set up an investment pool owned by the government with the idea of selling bonds to the Canadian people. I am opposed to that for many reasons, one of the principal ones being that I think it would place a large amount of money in the hands of the government which could be manipulated by government advisers to the detriment or disadvantage of industries and businesses in a way I should not like to see. In addition, it smacks to me too much of socialism.
Certainly there is nothing wrong with trying to convert the Canadian workingman into more of a capitalist by encouraging him to own a good percentage of Canadian industry. If I am right in my modest estimate of $100 per person invested by four or five million Canadians and if I am correct in my simple arithmetic that this means an investment potential of $400 or $500 million, and having in mind the apparent cure that this would be for most of our balance of payments problem, I may be forgiven for being somewhat critical of the government for not giving any consideration whatsoever to this in the budget resolutions.
To come back to where 1 started, I do not know where the minister got it but this conception of punitive measures to try to force people to hold shares rather than encouraging them through incentives is where we go wrong. I do not want to belabour the point too much. However, I suggest to the committee that my idea of trying to get Canadian working people to invest has one more aspect to it in that it does avoid the difficulties of anti-Americanism that showed up in the budget resolutions before, or the suggestion that might now be made that because the Liberals were so silly about putting this in in the first place they cannot now adequately make representations to the United States government to save us from the possible harmful effects envisaged in President Kennedy's message to congress.
We will be much less dependant on the inflow of foreign capital if we generate a lot more of our own. More than that, I suggest that we are going to earn the respect of other countries throughout the world if we learn to stand on our own two feet a little more. The simple fact is that today Canadians are spending a higher percentage of their wages on daily consumption than are most other people. To put it bluntly, Canadians are much more selfish as a people than the people of most other countries in the world. If you want to get ahead and stand on your own feet you must be prepared to make sacrifices. It is the duty of the government to encourage the Canadian people to make these sacrifices. It is the duty of the government to point out

to the Canadian people how helpful this would be, that all they have to do is to invest a little more.
I suggest that any scheme devised to get Canadians to invest more is bound to meet with failure if in the budget resolutions no encouragement is given to them and if in fact this aspect is ignored completely. How, 1 ask you, are Canadians to understand the basic difficulties of finance in this country if the government is going to ignore them in a budget which they themselves so loudly proclaim is to get the wheels of industry moving again.
I intend to speak on several items where specifically I think the opposite effect is achieved to what is desired. I believe that what is desired is to encourage more Canadian control of industry. It is not my understanding that this is a simple bookkeeping entry or that it is simply to discourage foreign investment. I believe that what the Minister of Finance had in mind was to bring in resolutions which would result in more Canadians investing money in Canadian industry, more Canadians owning Canadian industry, Canadians having a bigger share in Canadian industry, and making it more attractive to companies which now have money invested in Canada to have Canadians taking a bigger part than they now are. But I suggest this is unrealistic unless Canadians are going to dig into their own pockets and buy that percentage of industry. There is no such thing as holding a percentage in a different way in different companies. You might be able to influence things slightly but, boiled down, control and ownership in order to mean anything to the Canadian economy is investment control, the actual number of shares controlled and held by Canadians. We cannot do this until Canadians dig into their own pockets, and I suggest that we take another look at this resolution and encourage the Canadian workingman to start investing more.

Mr. Chairman, I am still a little worried about the use of the words "resident" and "non-resident" as they apply to shareholders and directors in this resolution. When I first asked the minister for a definition of "resident" he said he really did not know. He said later that it would be as the common law would indicate. This would seem to indicate that there must have been a tremendous amount of indecision in actually drawing up the budget resolutions. Since last speaking I have had a chance to look at some legal dictionaries and I should like to quote from The Dictionary of English Law by Earl Jowitt who was lord high chancellor of
Income Tax Act
Great Britain from 1945 to 1951. Under "residence" we find the following:
This word is used in law to denote the fact that a person dwells in a given place, or, in the case of a person, residence connotes the idea of carried on there: thus, if a company is formed in England for the purpose of carrying on a trade (such as mining or manufacturing) in a foreign country, but its business is under the control of a board of directors in England, the company is said to have its residence in England. In the case of a person, residence conotes the idea of home, or at least of habitation, and need not necessarily be permanent or exclusive. The word denotes the place where an individual eats, drinks and sleeps, or where his family or his servants eat, drink and sleep.
In another volume, Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, third edition, page 2569, the words "reside", "residence" and "resident" are dealt with, and I find the following:
"Residence" signifies a man's abode or continuance in a place. What is the meaning of the word "resides"? I take it that that word, where there is nothing to show that it is used in a more extensive sense, denotes the place where an individual eats, drinks and sleeps, or where his family or his servants eat, drink and sleep. A man's residence is where he habitually sleeps. "Residence" has a variety of meanings according to the statute or document in which it is used. It is an ambiguous word and may receive a different meaning according to the position in which it is found. The words "residence" and "place of abode" are flexible, and must be construed according to the object and intent of the particular legislation where they may be found. Primarily, they mean the dwelling and home where a man is supposed usually to live and sleep; they may also include a man's business abode, the place where he is to be found daily.
Then, there is a reference on page 2571 which refers to residence as regards income tax acts. There are a number of citations given there. I quote:
Domicil has here nothing to do with the meaning, for a man can have two or more residences in two or more different countries, but can have but one domicil; "residence", as regards income tax acts, has much the same meaning as in the Representation of the People Acts-
Then, farther along I find this:
Residence does not only mean residence on land; a residence, even by a foreigner, on his yacht anchored in English waters, suffices for liability to income tax; so also a man employed in Africa whose wife and family in Scotland received the bulk of his salary, was held to be a person residing in the United Kingdom, for purposes of income tax.
What I am suggesting to the minister is that the intention of this act, as expressed by other members, is in all probability to give greater preferment to Canadian investors and also to Canadian directors. I am satisfied that the way the provision is drawn now, without any definition coming from the minister as to residents or residence, practically any person who resides in Canada for even a short time could qualify for the purposes of the provision as it is now set out. The same situation

Income Tax Act
applies to a director. I feel that the definition which was previously requested should be given. If the words residents or residence are not sufficient, then some other words should be set forth. Would the minister now do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to thank the hon. member for what I feel is a very valuable contribution. I feel it is very helpful to have this explanation. I think perhaps he will agree that I was not too far off when I said this was a rather complicated subject. There is a lot of law on it with which I am unfamiliar, not being a member of his profession. I thank him for his contribution.

May I follow that up? The whole question is, do we get a definition or do we not? What was in the minister's mind when he introduced this in the budget, and also in the budget resolutions? We are today supposedly ready to pass this resolution, yet we have not got a definition. What I am suggesting here, as I have said before, is that Canadians get no preferment in any way, shape or form in so far as investment in Canada is concerned. In other words, practically anyone can qualify as long as he has a residence in Canada for ever so short a time.
I believe the same situation applies to a director. I asked the minister before if he had any figures as to the non-Canadian directors now resident in Canada and who are directors of firms which are controlled within the United States wholly or as subsidiaries. It is quite obvious that unless we do get some form of definition of residents or residence, or some binder on that in point of time, then we do not know where we stand at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member knows, in fact I am sure he does, that the Income Tax Act has been based on the concept of residence ever since it was first introduced in 1917. It has never been formally defined in the Income Tax Act, but it has been developed through a series of decisions. So far as I know, the whole act is based on this concept and this particular proposed resolution, which will be followed by a bill, follows the conception that has been developed. I suppose I should not say that it was the original concept when the income tax was introduced. There is no difference between residence in this case and residence under the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I might add to what the minister has said, I would refer the hon. member to section 139, subsection (3) of the Income Tax Act. There has been considerable jurisprudence developed on this particular section and also under the general law. It may be found in the Commercial Clearinghouse Service on Canadian Income Tax, in

McDonald on Canadian Income Tax-no relation-and the Deboo service, as well as many other services. Not only does the statute provide for this situation but defines the particular situation where a person is resident or non-resident, and that has been fully gone into by the Canadian tax courts. I think the answer to the hon. member's questions could be found there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to add a word of apology, if the members of the legal profession in the house will not misinterpret it. I understood that the hon. member was a member of the legal profession. I understand now that he is not. If he is not, I apologize for any misunderstanding.
Still a member of the profession, but not practising.

In so far as subparagraph A is concerned, I should like to put this question directly to the minister. In view of what has been said by other members, under formula A, if you can call it a formula, is it not possible for a foreigner or a group of foreigners residing in Canada, taking the idea of residence from other hon. members, to own a 25 per cent block of shares bought by foreign capital and qualify under formula A? In other words, a person may not be a Canadian citizen, but so long as he is residing in Canada and owns 25 per cent of the voting stock, even if it were brought with foreign capital, he could qualify under formula A. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

Well, I put the next question to the minister. Does the same situation not apply to formula B? In other words, is it not possible for a person residing in Canada to own these shares bought with foreign capital, and still qualify under formula B? In other words, this really does not encourage Canadians to make Canadian investments. Is that not the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can say is that it is based on residence and not citizenship.

If that is the situation, then I fail to see what the minister is trying to get at with this particular clause, this provision in the budget. If the purpose of the budget is to encourage Canadian participation, Canadian investors, in equity stocks, then residence, I put to the minister, is not the criterion. There are too many loopholes. All you have to do is have a company, a foreign company, and this applies whether it is British, French, Belgian or otherwise, or even in the West Indies where you have income tax at 2 per cent, and have the officers of the company residing here to

carry out the functions of directors. I know some companies that are domiciled there, and how they invest in Canada. The capital comes from there. All they do is send out officers of these companies who are residents while they are carrying out the functions, and the instructions come from the foreign firms; but they own the shares in the provincial companies that are established here, and these particular companies qualify for these exemptions.
It is true enough that the minister is encouraging investment in new facilities. That may be an incentive, but on the other hand I tell him in all sincerity that I do not think with this provision he will encourage Canadianization of equity capital if he is going to limit it to a residence qualification, because a residence qualification means nothing.
I suggest that if he wishes to guarantee the same end by introducing the concept of citizenship, then we would get somewhere more in keeping with the stated objectives of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a point of view. My own view is that that would be going too far at this stage.

I would like to put the
same question once again to the minister. First of all, it does not encourage Canadians to invest. It does not have to be Canadian capital. A foreigner residing in Canada can buy shares with foreign capital from another country, and he qualifies. Surely that is not the spirit of the budget?
