There has been an interesting discussion with regard to this resolution and we have dealt in general terms with the budget. In the last few minutes I think my cohorts got down to the gist and the meat of what is meant by this resolution, but first of all I would like to say a word or so of general comment with regard to the whole aspect of what we thought might be in the resolution and of what we had hoped would be in it.
The people of Canada were led to believe that our economy was stagnating in 1962 and early 1963. This is what the Liberal party told them, and the members of that party said they had to get the economy rolling again. I looked for something in the budget that would stimulate the economy and not hinder it, not drag it back, not control it and not limit it. To my amazement I found controls, limitations and hindrances and now, in dealing with this particular resolution, we see a great deal of nonsense because all the differentiating between paragraphs A and B is causing concern among companies and will accomplish very little for Canadians.
In 1962 we had a growth rate of 8 per cent in the gross national product. We were told this was not enough. We were also told unemployment was too high, and when the budget came along we looked for something which would increase Canada's growth rate and decrease unemployment, which were the announced intentions of the budget. But what do we see? We see an idea that Canadians should re-invest in Canada.
There are two ways through which this can be effected-through incentives and encouragement, or through controls and force. It reminds me of the old saying that you can lead a horse to water but you can't make him drink; and this is something of which the

Income Tax Act
minister should be well aware, because he tried several ideas in his budget. He has withdrawn some of them, and he is finding out that others will accomplish very little.
We see a great deal of confusion on the part of the government this afternoon with regard to the actual interpretation of the first part of the resolution. I think the hon. member for Bow River was quite correct when he said all one has to do is reside in Canada and own 25 per cent of a company to get the advantage of this part of the resolution. One does not have to become a citizen and take an active part in the development of the country, and there is no specified length of time for residence. As the hon. member for Bow River pointed out, many Americans are already residing in the city of Calgary.
The minister, when he was asked how the differentiation would be made, said 25 per cent of the voting shares would have to be beneficially owned. As I interpret this, it means it will be his decision to determine whether they are beneficially owned, and certainly if a person, company, association or group of persons have 25 per cent of the voting shares of a company operating in Canada we would hope it would be operating beneficially for Canada, and of course beneficially for themselves. These two tests, differentiating the way in which shares are held, actually amount to no real test. They give the minister very little guidance in using his judgment as to whether or not any given company is beneficial to Canada.
This is the way I interpret his remarks in this regard. He has tried to explain resolution No. 1 to the committee. He has done nothing but confuse the issue by perhaps not knowing just how these two tests will apply. The examples of Ford and General Motors have been used. One of these companies, under his category, is a good company and the other is bad. Surely the workers at General Motors feel they are getting paid just as well as those at Ford. In fact, perhaps there is more employment with General Motors than there is with Ford. They are both competing and making the same type of product, and surely if we are to tax either, they should be taxed on an equal basis. These companies are in the same business, employing the same number of people. I am sure the hon. member for Ontario, in whose city General Motors carries out its business, would have to say- and I am sure most of the residents of the city of Oshawa would have to say-that General Motors is very beneficial to Canada, Ontario and Oshawa.
How can the minister justify trying to bring about legislation and enactments under the Income Tax Act which will create in his

mind the good and the bad boys, and then it will be left to him alone to determine which company is good and which is bad. There is no real difference, as the hon. member for Bow River pointed out, between A and B, in a sense, in many cases. It is solely up to the minister to decide who is good and who is bad. I can remember that a few years ago, when there was certain legislation which the government was attempting to enact, with regard to which the minister was given discretion, the then opposition took strong exception and said the minister was given too great a prerogative. This resolution certainly gives the minister a far greater prerogative. All these resolutions hinge upon the minister's decision as to what is beneficial and whether or not a company meets his two tests, which are in a sense one test.
It was suggested earlier that resolution No. 1 should be stood. I wholeheartedly agree, because even the minister and his officials are not clear as to how it would apply; they are not clear about its administrative effects. This is not the first time the minister has brought in items which he has not thoroughly thought out. The whole budget of June 13 has become a shambles because this has been withdrawn this, that and the other have been changed. We have seen that on June 13 he made part of paragraph 4 retroactive to April 10, 1962. Now he takes the retroactive part away. He says, "We have to take this away now; certain companies might benefit". At page 1498 of Hansard he said they had to make it retroactive to April 10, 1962 because some very complicated drafting would have to be carried out if it were to be made effective on the day of the presentation of the budget. He now makes it effective on June 13. I did not see any of the complicated drafting that he said was necessary on June 24. However, the minister seems to have that faculty which is given to most of the fairer sex, of being able to change his mind at will and often enough to keep everybody in the country, including the officials, in a state of flux, in a state where they hardly know where they are with regard to the budget, with regard to these income tax resolutions, with regard to whether or not the economy is being asked to forge ahead or stagnate.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these resolutions, together with other parts of the budget, will do nothing to stimulate the economy or promote employment in the country. They will cause unemployment and bring about a loss of investment in the country, which will come anyway because of the recent announcement by President Kennedy as to taxing investment in Canada by United States persons. Certainly we see nothing in this particular resolution which will aid the economy. I agree with other

hon. members, and particularly the financial critic of the opposition, who said that this resolution should be stood at least until the minister becomes clear as to where he is trying to go with this basic idea that Canadians should invest in Canada. We certainly agree with the principle that Canadians should invest in Canada, but you cannot force them to do so; you can create the incentive for them to invest. Without fully thought out suggestions, without fully thought out budgets, without fully thought out income tax resolutions this house can hardly be asked to pass these measures when the minister and the officials are not certain what they mean by them. I suggest that this resolution be stood at least until the minister becomes clear on it and can clarify the position to the house and the country with regard to where he wants this particular theme of his projected across the country.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to raise a very small difficulty or problem that has been put to me and ask the Minister of Finance something about it. I have had complaints from several small accountants, people who do work in smaller towns for individual taxpayers in preparing their income tax returns and also do considerable work for small businesses which happen to be incorporated companies, that one of the effects of these regulations will be to deprive them of a considerable amount of work, in that it will concentrate in the same season of the year, the same time, the activity that in a sense they have been carrying on throughout the year for these small business organizations.
I do not know how important this is, but it was put to me that it was another example of the kind of regulation that will cause no immediate hardship, after the first instance, to the large corporation which has at its disposal a well geared financial reporting organization. It will cause no disadvantage, and indeed it will be of assistance, to chartered accountant firms which are large in size, which have a number of employees, juniors and people whom they are training. But for the individual accountant, or the person who may not be qualified as an accountant but is making his living through doing this kind of work, usually with some kind of banking or clerical experience, this is going to be a very severe blow, the kind of blow that perhaps will not be felt in the big cities but, let us say, amongst the small business people across the country.
I do not know how significant is this criticism, but the bitterness with which it was expressed suggests to me that perhaps the minister could give some indication as to
Income Tax Act
whether the effect of this has been considered and just how important or telling the criticism may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the point the hon. member has raised has to do with paragraph 15 of the resolution. I have received a number of representations on this point. The objective of the clause, as the hon. member pointed out, is to get the money in earlier rather than to make life complicated for the people who make up the return. I am looking into the matter and hope to be able to do something about it.

Mr. Chairman, on the issue of the small town accountant to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred-I think I know to what he was referring-I was pleased to hear the minister say that he proposes to do something about it. Also, as a small town accountant I have come to one very sincere conclusion, and that is simply that ownership cannot be legislated for. I do not believe it is possible to do so.
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister concerning the actual application of this section. For argument's sake, let us say some machinery or plant is purchased within the two year period. The company is to be limited to writing off this machinery and plant over a period of two years. I think the minister said this morning that it would not be necessary for the firm actually to write it off over a period of two years; but 1 am wondering, for argument's sake, if a new firm, which normally would not show a profit in the first year or two, chose not to write it off, what would happen at the end of the two year period? Would they then be able to write it off under the terms of the act as they now exist, or could they write it off at 50 per cent a year, presuming that they did not wish to start writing it off until after the end of the two year period?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was interested in hearing the hon. member refer to himself as a small town accountant, or an accountant from a small town. I seem to remember that at one time he and I were students in the same firm and he did not give any indication then that there was anything "small town" about him at all. In fact, just the reverse.
Do not give away secrets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will not give away any more secrets, but I remember that life was very pleasant in those days. Let me assure him on that point. As I said to the hon. member for Port Arthur, this matter is under study, and probably before the bill comes along we may be able to do something about it. With

Income Tax Act
regard to the second point he raised about the depreciation or the capital cost allowance, it somebody does not choose to write it off at that rate over the first two years then they can write it off as fast as they like afterwards.
They can still write it off at the end of the two year period, and following the end of the two year period?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, as long as the investment has been made in this period.

Mr. Chairman, on the point made by the hon. gentleman opposite with respect to changing the concept of the Income Tax Act from one of residence to one of domicile or citizenship, I would point out that this would also involve persons who were resident in Canada but were not citizens or domiciled here, but who would be able to live here, earn their incomes here and pay no income tax. I trust that our hon. friends opposite are not trying to create a state of preferred citizens in this way.

In reply to that, I think the hon. member for Renfrew South was referring to my observations in this regard. I am not suggesting that under the general concept of the Income Tax Act we should remove ourselves from the residence provision, which says that everyone who is resident in Canada for a period of 183 days or more is thereupon subject to income tax. There may be some other exceptions in the fine print of other regulations which may catch other persons; but what I am concerned about is this: Bearing in mind the objectives of the budget, the incentive to invest in new facilities can apply to anybody. That I accept. But the further objective of encouraging Canadian investment I do not think is accomplished by the wording of this resolution or this requirement. You could have a person who was a citizen of the world who could bring in capital, which capital could be hidden. I noticed that the parliamentary secretary was dubitant, shall I say, that the matter of beneficial ownership would cover this. But let me assure him that it is quite easy to hide true ownership. Certainly from my three years connection with the Department of National Revenue I know that the minister and his able senior civil servants in the department had not the personnel to delve into all these cases and really track them down. As a lawyer I can assure the hon. member that capital can be hidden. Remember that we are giving certain people an advantage in the act. In order to qualify for this advantage, why would you not require that it be limited to citizens if your objective is the Canadianization of equity holdings in Canadian corporations? In order to gain this

advantage, surely to goodness one has to put up something too. That is my point.

I should like to ask the minister one further question on this business of the actual write off. Frankly, not having been in practice for some years I have forgotten the appropriate term, but I will put it this way. When you have written off a new piece of machinery in two years and you then choose to sell that piece of machinery or trade it in, what happens to the capital value?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is subject to recapture. I do not know whether that is the term that is used, but that is what it means.

One other question on paragraph 1(b), which says:
-a corporation that on the last day of the year was a corporation with a degree of Canadian ownership and control.
Then it goes on to explain the ownership and control, and so on. What would happen if, for argument's sake, a company which had been a United States partnership were in Canada and it was not a corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be dealt with under 1(a).

Mr. Chairman, there was
some discussion between the minister and myself this afternoon with reference to the statement that if we had less than 3 per cent unemployment he would take issue with me. I should like to put on record what his exact words were in "Troubled Canada". I might say in respect to the minister that he showed me what he said in the Gordon report.
Who is the author?

The author, of course, is the present Minister of Finance. Starting on page 3 he says:
Our primary aim, therefore, which for the time being should take precedence over all other objectives no matter how desirable they are, must be to stimulate and encourage economic activity throughout Canada, to re-establish a satisfactory rate of annual growth, and to restore high levels of employment.
All those aims are very honourable. Then this is the paragraph:
This does not mean that every single man and woman in Canada would be employed every day all through the year.
There will always be some people who are in the process of changing jobs or who are engaged in seasonal pursuits or who have decided not to work for a few months for some reason or another, or who come under the category of "unemployable".
After, saying that he said this-and I think you have to read that with this:
If the number of people without jobs for these reasons could be reduced to even 3 or 4 per cent

of the total working force, this would mean that only half as many people would be out of work as in 1960. This would be a great accomplishment.
In other words, he says there will always be people who are changing their jobs, who are out of work because they follow seasonal pursuits or who refuse to work for one reason or another. For example, a man may have worked on a big construction job in the summer and decides to draw unemployment insurance in the winter. Note what the hon. gentleman says, that it would be a great accomplishment if the number of these people were reduced by half. In other words, if this could be done he would be satisfied.
Oh, oh.
Well, if he does not say that, it is a matter of interpretation. I have at least put on record what he said in his book, "Troubled Canada".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am delighted to have it on record. What I was saying at that time was that if unemployment could be reduced by 50 per cent it would represent a great improvement. If it could be reduced by 75 per cent it would be a still greater improvement.
I wonder if I might refer to something which was said earlier about any possible connection between the budget resolutions we are now discussing and the recent proposals of President Kennedy. I think all hon. members would like to know that the state department has formally denied today that President Kennedy's proposed tax on the purchase of foreign securities by United States citizens and residents is a retaliatory measure against Canada. Mr. Robert J. McCloskey said that in Canadian circles there had been some suggestion that the Kennedy measures were directed specifically at Canada or had been taken in retaliation for the action proposed by the Canadian authorities earlier. This is absolutely not the case, Mr. McCloskey said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Port Arthur.
I should like to make one remark to the minister with reference to what he said about unemployment.
I will yield to the hon. member if continuity requires it.

Actually, I had two things I wished to say. I heard over the radio today that there are 30,000 more people unemployed in Canada today than there were a year ago. That information seems to have come from the dominion bureau of statistics.
With regard to the position some of us took on this side on this question of possible
Income Tax Act
retaliation as far as the United States administration is concerned, what I, myself, said was that the action taken by the hon. gentleman would make it more difficult to negotiate with the United States administration with reference to the new proposed tax. Having taken the position we did in the budget we can hardly go along and say to the United States government: This measure is going to make it very difficult for Canada; it is likely to increase unemployment here and make it harder for us in one way or another. There is no doubt it will be more difficult for us. For example, we only have to look at what happened to bond issues today. I think they fell four points. It will be much more difficult now for the Minister of Finance to negotiate with the administration and say: please take this tax back. After all, we planned to do to them something which was worse than what they now plan to do to us.
May I suggest that the hon. member's party is hardly the party to tell us how to negotiate with the United States.
The hon. member for Renfrew South obviously does not know what he is talking about.

I wanted to ask the minister a question about the over-all intention of these resolutions in trying to do something about Canadian ownership. I have not been able to find any statement by the minister regarding the problem raised by mutual funds and mutual fund companies, so many of which are operating in Canada with aggressive sales forces under United States control. The principle which seems inherent in mutual funds operations is that because of the need to keep shifting and balancing their portfolios and also because of certain regulations it is not the policy of mutual fund groups to exercise any ownership claim in respect of their shares in terms of controlling management policy.
As I understand it, these groups are becoming increasingly important in the investment market and their business has been expanding rapidly in Canada. I wonder whether the minister or his officials have considered at any time in the preparation of this budget whether this denial on the part of mutual funds or holding companies of their right to exert in certain circumstances their ownership privileges is, at the same time, a denial of the intent inherent in this legislation. Also, is it not the case that here the government has perhaps an opportunity to find a vehicle which might be used for Canadian ownership purposes as seems to be intended by this act?
I am interested in this matter because we advocate some kind of Canadian development

Income Tax Act
fund which, I understand, is within the framework of the thinking of the minister himself. In essence, if we have a development fund we are tapping the potential for equity investment in Canada today and doing it through these mutual investment funds, and it would seem to me there is an opportunity here, and I should like to have the minister's comments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not clear what the point of the hon. members question is. If he is talking about mutual funds, they would qualify under this proposal if 25 per cent of their stock was listed and available for purchase by Canadian investors. I do not know if that was his point or not.

That was part of it, but my point was that these companies are important and also vulnerable, since ownership does not mean anything in terms of the actual management of companies. What they are interested in is the income, not management policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sufficiently familiar with mutual funds to know what the significance is of the difference between the ownership and the management contract. I presume that in the final analysis the owners must be able to change the contract unless it is a very long term contract. I just do not know. I would be glad to talk to the hon. member later or now, but I do not think there is very much more I can add at this moment.

On this particular point, I am rather pleased that we have come back to the question of mutual funds or the participation of Canadian investors in American or foreign controlled mutual funds which have investments in Canada. This is a point which I think creates some difficulty, and it is quite conceivable that the minister may have the answer.
Let us assume that company X is a public company resident in Canada and operating in Canada, and it desires to avail itself of the benefits proposed in the first paragraph with respect to depreciation. Part of the shareholdings are taken up by a mutual fund in which Canadians participate. However, the mutual fund is an American or foreign investment group. How does this company qualify under this provision? I do not know whether you are going to go one step beyond by looking at the ownership of the mutual fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It qualifies under section B if its stock is listed on a Cnadian stock exchange, irrespective of who owns the stock. It does not matter who owns it. If it is listed on a Canadian stock exchange, then Canadians have an opportunity to buy the stock at some

price, and under those circumstances it qualifies. But it does not matter whether there is a mutual fund or any other owner of the shares.
In other words, it is the listing that counts.

Is that not the solution to the minister's problem? Is it not the listing which will accomplish almost as much as any of these other qualifications? I was rather intrigued a moment ago by his reply to the hon. member dealing with when this depreciation should be taken. Frankly, I thought it had to be within the first two years. I guess I have not read the section very carefully.
I listened to the minister this morning and he said, I think quite properly, that there was need for the improvement and modernizing of industrial plant and equipment and that this was an incentive to that end. It was my impression that the incentive was going to be on a do it now, do not wait, basis. But now we are told that, provided they buy up, they can take the depreciation at any time. Obviously the provision is not an incentive for employment because the only people who can get the benefit of this are those who qualify under these technical provisions in so far as control is concerned. It is not to improve over-all employment as it would be if we gave an incentive to General Motors and Ford, such as I mentioned a few moments ago.
Frankly, I am wondering now just what the intention of the section is after the dialogue, shall I say, that we have had back and forth during the day. I am not clear in my mind as to what the intention is. As the hon. member for Edmonton West said a moment ago, could not the same thing be achieved by saying that the company must be registered or listed on a Canadian stock exchange? I think the minister would accomplish almost as much as he would by these various qualifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry if I did not make it clear to the hon. member. The incentive and the urge are to encourage these particular companies to increase their investment in plant and machinery, and naturally in the process to do two things, to modernize their plants and to provide employment either in the primary or secondary sense, either in their own plants or for the people who build the plants or produce the machinery. The objective and intention are to get this work done within the next two years. The purpose of that, of course, is to provide more employment within the next two years. The incentive that is offered is a 50 per cent

write-off, but the date when the write-off is taken does not make much difference as long as the work is done within the first tew years. That is the first point that the hon. member raised.
As to the second point, the people who qualify for this will be either, under A, those companies where there is a 25 per cent beneficial ownership in Canada or, B, where Canadians have the opportunity to acquire up to 25 per cent. That means that the stock must be listed on an exchange and that no single parent company or groups of parent companies should control more than 75 per cent. The theory behind this is that if there is 25 per cent around, Canadians can buy it at some price.

Could I ask the minister a supplementary question in connection with depreciation? Was consideration given to allowing the special depreciation write-off for machinery or equipment of a class or kind made in Canada rather than on the very general basis set out here? I suspect there might have been some consideration given to that and I am wondering what comment the minister has to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It could be done that way, but if one of our objectives is to see that Canadian industry becomes as efficient and modern as possible I think it perhaps would be unwise to limit this incentive just to machinery of a class or kind made in Canada. I should like to see more machinery made in Canada, as I am sure the hon. member would; but there are some kinds of machinery that we all know are not obtainable in Canada and yet our industry will need the best machinery in the world if it is going to be able to compete with other countries in the world.

With regard to the acquisition of plant or equipment, does this mean a firm contract for purchase and delivery maybe two years and six months hence, or must it be delivered and installed before the second anniversary? You can enter into a firm contract for the erection of a very complicated industrial plant, say an oil refinery or something of that nature, which takes more than two years to plan and instal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the test is the acquisition of title.

Mr. Chairman, if I can change the point a little, the minister mentioned the statement by the United States state department that their action was not a retaliatory measure. The mere fact that they should feel it necessary to issue such a statement rather alarms me because I am one of those who talked about the effect our proposed action
Income Tax Act
might have had on the Americans, and I certainly did not want anything I said to be construed that way by the Americans or anyone else. I know that my leader took the same position and I am sure from what he said that it was not to be construed that this could by any stretch of the imagination be taken as a retaliatory measure or that the Americans were being accused of this.
When there is this sort of misunderstanding I think it is necessary that I should say something about it, because I know that too many statements made by this party have, in some inexplicable way, been construed as anti-American when they were not intended to be. Just to set the record straight I should like to explain to the house and to our American friends that the action taken by them is not considered by us or anyone else, I am sure, as retaliatory. I wish to make it clear that my remarks about the action we took having misled the Americans in some way meant only that I can understand that the government, having brought in such measures, might have misled the Americans to believe they could have been mistaken about any harmful effects they might have foreseen in their legislation, or we would not take this sort of action. The United States may say we prepared for this sort of thing. My hon. friends may say to the United States, we are going on a new facet of investment handling on both sides. We have our own reasons, which again mislead the United States into believing that these harmful effects would not prevail.
Then, next, I made this point very clear, for which I hope I may be forgiven, that the government, having made an initial mistake and having put in this measure originally, and then having to withdraw it because it was going to be so harmful to us and because it caused so much resentment in the United States, just indicates that this government had so little understanding or was so callous of the effect it had on the United States that this government was put in the position where it had practically tied its hands in trying to explain to the United States how harmful President Kennedy's proposal might be.
This is so on the following grounds; One, that this government had no hesitation in doing something similar and, two, this government had so little understanding of it that it would do it anyway. Therefore, any protest made by this government might arise out of that same sort of ignorance of the consequences, and this could have done nothing but weaken the position of this government in making its protestation. I am sure that in all of this there is nothing our United States friends can construe as any accusation whatever that it is retaliatory. In fact, I thought

Income Tax Act
the explanation we made was explanatory of the United States action, and how the action of this government could have resulted in what might, at first blush, be taken to be a sort of anti-Canadian action by the United States. We did not call it anti-Canadian; we were merely explaining what this government might have done to lead the United States into thinking this would not harm us, and why this government is not now in any position to adequately explain our position to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to assure the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona that I did not mean to imply that any of his remarks had made a particular impact on President Kennedy or even on the controller of the treasury. I do remind him that just before one o'clock I went out of my way, in referring to the remarks of his leader, to say that I was quite certain that the Leader of the Opposition had not in any way said anything that could have been interpreted in that way, or if he had, he had not meant it. I think perhaps, therefore, we can let the matter rest there.
I suppose that by this time most hon. members know that there have been reports from Washington, I do not know how authentic they are, that the treasury has said the measure will not come into effect now until August 16.
You have company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are various suggestions that the measure will be modified, changed, clarified or amended as sometimes happens with complicated measures of this kind. I think, too, hon. members will know by this time of statements made by the state department in answer to any suggestion that this measure was in any way retaliatory. I can assure my hon. friend from Edmonton-Strathcona that this government is in an excellent position to negotiate with the United States on this and all other matters.

Obviously, Mr. Chairman, they have so much in common in shifting and changing their ground with respect to financial matters that they are, perhaps, in a very good position to negotiate on these things.
I should like to go back to a question I raised with the minister a few moments ago. I gathered from him that the primary objective of this measure was the renovation of Canadian plants and equipment. I did not have that impression when we started. I thought the objective was to increase employment and to provide for Canadianization. I understood that it was, also, indirectly to provide for the renovation of plants and equipment. Then, the minister made it very plain, I think, that the primary objective of

the provision in question, as he told me a few minutes ago, was the renovation of plant and equipment.
If that is the case, I cannot understand why it is tied up with the necessity for a degree of Canadian ownership. It may be, of course, that the subsidiaries are so wealthy that the parent company need not put up the money. However, I believe there are a good many here who cannot. I do think it is unfortunate as a matter of tactics, and I do not say this critically, that so far as the incentive is concerned the depreciation is tied up with Canadian ownership. We could have dealt with it much more quickly than we have if the depreciation had not been tied to a degree of Canadian ownership. The minister says the purpose of the section is simply the renovation of plant and improving the efficiency of Canadian industry. If it is, then the provision should apply to all companies in Canada, whether they are owned by people in the United States, the Dutch, Germans or Canadians.
I suggest again that there must be a dual purpose in this provision. If a company obtains what we term a degree of Canadian ownership, then it is going to get this and if it does not it will not. This vitiates entirely the argument of the minister that the primary purpose of this provision is to improve efficiency. If you are going to Canadianize these firms, that is one thing. Let us say so. Let us not say it is to increase renovation, and then tie that up with this other matter which, so far as I am concerned and a good many others on this side, is not a happy move. We do not like to accept it. If it had been purely a matter of depreciation, and if it had not been tied up with this description of Canadian ownership, then the provision would have gone through much more quickly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does this complete discussion on paragraph 1?

Six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the house leader let us know what the program may be for next week?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I can put it very simply; budget resolutions and still more budget resolutions and then the bills. When these have been completed, I will be able to satisfy the hon. gentleman's curiosity about other matters.

Statement By
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, Honourable Judy LaMarsh Respecting the Canada Pension Plan
July 18, 1963
The purpose of the government's proposed legislation is to ensure that, as soon as is possible in a fair and practical way, all Canadians will be able to retire in security and with dignity.
The advantage of a federal plan is that it is the only type of pension plan that can be made available comprehensively to all Canadians. This was recognized in 1951 when the British North America Act was amended. The Canada pension plan is comprehensive in this sense. It will mean that a contributory program is available to Canadians to provide for their old age. Coverage will be compulsory for, broadly, all employees; such exceptions as are made will be for those types of employment in which the collection of contributions is not administratively feasible. Most other people having earned incomes- broadly, the self employed and the majority of employees not covered compulsorily-will be able to belong to the plan voluntarily. If a provincial government wishes, its employees will be covered.
The Canada pension plan is not intended to be comprehensive in any other sense; it is not designed to provide all the retirement income which many Canadians wish to have. This is a matter of individual choice and, in the government's view, should properly be left to personal savings and to private pension plans, subject in the latter case to such degree of supervision as the provinces may think appropriate. The recent Ontario legislation is the first example in Canada of an attempt at close supervision of private plans.
The purpose of the Canada pension plan is to make reasonable minimum levels of income available to all Canadians at normal retirement ages. There will be scope for the continuation and extension of private pension plans to provide benefits over these minimum levels.
The present minimum provided in Canada is the old age security benefit of $65 a month from age 70. Unfortunately many people are unable to go on earning until they reach age 70.
Realistic minimum levels of pensions cannot be achieved, in a country like Canada, simply by increasing the flat rate pension. Living costs vary greatly between town and country, and between different regions of Canada. What people need, in order to make satisfactory provision for retirement, is related in part to the level of earnings to which they have been accustomed. The Canada pension plan will therefore both increase the flat rate benefit and provide new levels of pensions related to previous earnings.
Main Features
The Canada pension plan will make these main changes in the provision of pensions:
1.	The flat rate pension will be raised to $75 at age 70 for everyone who meets the residence requirements of the Old Age Security Act.
2.	People whose pensions begin after the plan is in operation will receive, if they have made contributions under the plan, a further pension in proportion to the earnings on which they have been contributing. The scale of pensions will rise during a ten year transitional period.
3.	The increased flat rate pension and the earnings related pension will both be available at any age between 65 and 70, according to the preference of the pensioner. The amount of both pensions will be graduated so that anyone with average life expectancy will receive the same total payment, from the age he starts his pension to the time he dies, whatever starting age he chooses.
The main features in the financing of the plan are:
4.	Since the new benefits will be related to earnings, the Canada pension plan will be financed by contributions of a percentage of earnings. The rate of contribution during the ten year transition period will not exceed 2 per cent of the earnings on which contributions are made. For wage and salary earners, the employer will be required to pay a half of this contribution.

5.	Initially contributions will be made, and benefits will be paid, on the first $4,000 of annual earnings. This level will be raised in line with any increase in average earnings.
6.	Contributions will be deductible from taxable income. This is the same as for private pension plans.
7.	The Canada pension plan will be entirely self financing. The contributions are designed to cover all pension costs over and above the continuation of the existing $65 pension at age 70. The cost of administration will also be covered from the contributions.
Timing
It will take a good part of a year to set up satisfactorily the administrative machinery for collecting contributions under the plan. Graduated pensions cannot be paid until the contributor has a record of earnings as the base for determining the rate of benefit. Graduated pensions will therefore begin in January 1966. Contributions before this date will be used to finance the earlier addition of $10 to flat rate pensions.
In January 1966 two things will happen. The plan will begin to provide pensions related to earnings. People will become able to start drawing pensions, both flat rate and earnings related, before age 70.
Until the plan is ten years old, pension rates will build up steadily. In 1966 the graduated benefit at age 70 will be $10 a month for anyone who retires after contributing on earnings of $4,000 a year. For anyone retiring in 1967 the maximum will be $20 a month, and so on until the top rate of $100 a month is reached after ten years. For people with lower earnings, the benefits will be proportional to these. The flat rate pension of $75 will, of course be available in addition to the graduated benefit. The amounts available in total pensions will therefore rise from $75 to people already retired to $175 for contributors with average earnings of $4,000 in 1975.
Financing
The Canada pension plan will not build up a huge investment fund in the hands of the federal government. Instead, it will be financed on a pay as you go basis. The money received in contributions will in most years approximately match the money paid out to pensioners. While the program will operate with a contingency reserve, in order to avoid short run fluctuations in contribution rates, this reserve will normally be small by comparison with the size of the annual payments.
This method of financing is a fundamental difference between a public pension plan and
private plans. While full funding may be provided under private pension plans, it is not the practice in government old age insurance programs. Indeed, full funding on the scale of a nation-wide plan would be a quite excessive form of saving enforced by the state.
The practical consequence is that this plan can provide benefits within a few years-to people whose working lives are already well advanced-whereas a private plan ordinarily provides good pensions only to people who join the plan when they are quite young.
Contributions under the plan will not be required before the age of 18. They will stop at whatever age, between 65 and 70, a pension benefit is taken.
The initial contribution rates will be adequate for the financing of the plan through the transition years. The rate will slowly rise for about a generation afterward, as the plan matures and an increasing proportion of people have retired at the full rate of graduated pension.
The ratio of benefits to contributions is especially favourable for those who retire during the transition period. It is therefore reasonable during this period to assess the voluntary contributor at or close to the combined employer and employee rate. However, after the program has been in operation for a period of time and adjustments have to be made in contribution rates, the rate paid by voluntary contributors may be less than the combined rate for employer and employee.
Calculation of Benefits
Pensions are to be 30 per cent, adjusted if the starting age is before 70, of "what a man has been earning."
This obviously cannot mean what the pensioner earned in, say, the last year or even few years before beginning the pension. That would be very unfair to the man who suffered sickness or unemployment in the last few years before retirement. On the other hand, the pensioner cannot be allowed to pick the best year or few years of his earnings record; that would excessively favour the man whose earnings have been erratic and it would tempt voluntary contributors to contribute only in good years.
The pension benefit will therefore be based on the man's average earnings from the effective date of the plan to the time when he starts to draw his pension. These earnings cannot, however, be used without adjustment. To do so would mean that, as the general level of earnings rises over the years, there would be a widening span between earnings recorded in the early years and those shortly before retirement. The pension benefits paid

would therefore be a declining proportion of "what a man has been earning" shortly before retirement.
Accordingly, for calculating pensions, earnings will be adjusted in line with changes in the general level of salaries and wages. The current average of salaries and wages in Canada is about $4000 a year, the ceiling chosen for earnings under the Canada pension plan. This ceiling will also be adjusted with changes in the general level of wages and salaries. The pension program will therefore permanently provide a satisfactory standard of pensions for people with earnings up to the average level.
If a man starts his pension in, say, 1970, "what he has been earning" will be calculated by averaging his actual earnings in 1969 and, for each earlier year, his earnings adjusted by the change in average salaries and wages between that year and 1969. In other words, all his earnings will be put on a 1969 equivalent.
The use of average earnings would excessively penalize people whose earnings in some years are abnormally low because of sickness and unemployment. This will be overcome, to a reasonable degree, by excluding a man's years of lowest earnings from the calculation of his average earnings. Also, for each year beyond 65 that a man continues to work, he will be able to exclude, from the calculation of his average earnings, an additional low year. This will provide quite a powerful incentive to go on working after 65 for the man who is able to do so, without any large reduction in pay.

Adjustment for Age
Pensions drawn before the age of 70 will be reduced by a small percentage for each
month between the date when the pension starts and the date of the pensioner's seventieth birthday. For anyone who takes his pension at the earliest opportunity, when he reaches 65, the pension received would be 32.5 per cent less than the pension he could have claimed at age 70. This reduction at ages between 65 and 70 would be proportional to this.
Anyone who is eligible for both the flat rate and the graduated pension must choose the same age for starting both.
There will be no retirement test. A man may start drawing the appropriate rate of pension at any time between his 65th and 70th birthdays, whatever his other earnings. Once he elects to draw his pension he cannot go off pension for a while and then come back on at a higher rate.

The income available to the surviving partner of a marriage will be rather more than half the previous combined income of the couple. To achieve this, since the flat rate pension is halved, the income related pension available to a widow will be 60 per cent of the benefit available to the couple.
This provision will apply with equality to the sexes. That is, it applies equally to either a widow or, if a deceased wife had earned income entitling her to a pension, to a widower.

Administration
The Department of National Health and Welfare will administer the Canada pension plan. The contributions under the plan will be collected by the Department of National Revenue. Employers will be responsible for deductions from their employees and will then remit these deductions monthly, together with their own contributions, to that department. Voluntary participants will make annual payments to the department.
The Department of National Health and Welfare will maintain an index of contributors, and will be responsible for the payment of benefits. The Department of National Revenue will forward to the Department of National Health and Welfare the record of pensionable earnings so that this information can be credited to each individual contributor's account. The maintenance of the records and the calculation of benefits will be achieved through the use of modern data processing equipment.
The necessary provisions will be made for appeal procedures to ensure that contributors, beneficiaries and employers may have an impartial review of any disputes which may arise in relation to the program.
Authority will be provided to work out reciprocal agreements with other countries for the coverage of people who move between countries.
Relation to Other Pension Plans
A great contribution to old age security has been made, and will continue to be made, by the considerable growth of private pension plans, which now cover more than 1,800,000 people in Canada. Not all of these plans, however, provide sizeable pensions, particularly for workers who do not join the plan early in life. Also, since vesting is rarely complete, private plans have operated as a growing restraint on the mobility of labour.
Several provinces are interested in lessening these and other problems connected with private pension plans, particularly by the establishment of rules for portability and solvency. These are, in the view of the federal government, useful steps forward.
However, since such private plans would be funded, even their compulsory extension cannot make possible retirement at an adequate standard for people now in their forties to sixties who have not been covered previously. Moreover, self employed people cannot have access to such plans.
The Canada pension plan not only provides early benefits but also automatically provides Canada wide portability of pensions for people with earnings up to an average level. It is thus designed for those whose needs
cannot be fully met by the extension of private pension plans under provincial supervision. It will be available comprehensively and it will quickly provide fair sized pensions to those who retire in the next decade or two.
The plan is designed to meet these needs of the Canadian people while helping to establish a pension system which, through the combination of private, provincial and federal action, will be sound and satisfactory in the long run.
The Adjustment Period
The adjustment of private pension plans to a public program with graduated benefits cannot be altogether easy. However, this does not appear to have been a deterrent to private plans in the United States. Since the American Old Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance program was established there has continued to be a substantial growth in private pension plans. The number of employees covered by private pension plans, expressed as a percentage of the wage and salary workers in private industry, rose from 31 per cent in 1954 to 45 per cent in 1961 in the United States.
The Canada pension plan has been designed to ease as fully as possible the adjustment of private pension plans to the developing public program. The fact that the Canada pension plan will be financed on a pay as you go basis, with a small contingency reserve, ensures that contributions in the early years of the program are at a very modest level. The absence of large reserves means that there will not be large transfers of funds from the private sector to the public sector of the economy. Transfers will be from the working population and employers to retired people, who will spend their benefits largely on consumer expenditures. It is not proposed that large reserves be built up as a vehicle for federal debt management and public investment.
Some employers and employees will no doubt wish to revise existing pension plans by reducing contribution rates approximately in line with their contributions under the Canada Pension Plan. The ten-year transitional period means that such adjustments can be made carefully and gradually.
In sum, the advantages of the fairly lengthy transition are:
1.	To provide adequate time for existing pension plans to be adjusted to the federal plan;
2.	To enable contribution rates to begin at a low level and rise fairly slowly, so that companies and individuals not now paying into pension schemes will have time to adjust to this new financial situation;

3.	To avoid too sharp a contrast between people who have already retired-who will get the new $75 minimum pension-and people who start drawing pensions only a few years later.
Economic Progress
In the government's view, the great merit of the Canada pension plan is that it is a social security program which is realistically geared to the growth of the economy. It can help to provide a foundation for their social programs, notably for those who are disabled, for widows with dependant children and for orphans. In itself, it quickly makes modest pensions available. These benefits will grow until, in ten years, an adequate scale of pensions is available for people of low and moderate incomes. As such incomes grow, with economic progress, the scale will rise in a way which ensures that people who make contributions now can be assured of pensions which will still provide a secure retirement in line with the economic conditions of the time.
In the growth of the economy, importance is rightly placed on the role of private pension plans in providing savings to finance investment. All pension arrangements, of course, require payments out to the beneficiaries as well as savings by those who are now working. In a static economy no mature pension plan would be in itself a source of savings. The net saving through private pension plans arises from the growth of the plans as the population increases and income levels rise.
Such growth is of continued importance. The Canada pension plan will provide, on a permanent basis, the scale of pensions for low and moderate incomes which is an appropriate first charge on a society that values the security and dignity of those whose working life is past. But there will remain full scope for private saving above this minimum. The scope will be enlarged with economic progress. The individual, in association in many cases with his employer, will remain responsible for the saving which a rich and growing country needs for its further economic development, and by which more and more people can afford to provide for themselves a truly comfortable retirement.

RELATED PROGRAMS Survivors and Disabled Pensions
A full program of social insurance would provide benefits for survivors and disabled persons who have not reached an age at which benefit would normally be considered an old age pension. Doubts have been expressed whether such benefits are within federal jurisdiction under the existing provisions of the British North America Act. Certainly such programs as now exist for these people are provincially administered. This is, accordingly, a subject which requires full consultation and discussion between federal and provincial governments to ascertain the wishes of the provinces and to determine whether a mutually satisfactory approach can be worked out.
The persons who might be covered under wage related pensions for survivors and disabled persons would be as follows:

(a)	Widows with dependant children
A pension payable from the date of the death of a contributor to his widow, if she has one or more dependant children, until the youngest child reaches age 18.
(b)	Orphans
A pension payable in respect of the orphans of a contributor from the date of death of the last surviving parent until the youngest orphan reaches age 18.
(c)	Disabled Persons
A pension payable to a contributor under the program who suffers such a prolonged disability that he is unable to secure gainful employment.
If such coverage were to be provided as an additional part of the Canada pension plan, the scale of pensions would be related to the benefit otherwise available to the contributor at age 65, and the cost of the benefits would be financed as a part of the contributory program.
Federal-Provincial Shared Programs
Another related matter concerns federal-provincial assistance programs. The introduction of an adjusted pension at age 65 will
reduce federal-provincial expenditures under the old age assistance program. Once the Canada pension plan is in operation many persons in the 65 to 69 age group will not have to seek old age assistance because the adjusted benefits will be available. Similarly, if a disability pension is subsequently included as a part of the Canada pension plan, many persons who would otherwise have sought assistance through blind persons or disabled persons allowances will find their needs met under the new program.
Since payment of old age assistance, blind persons and disabled persons allowances is made by the provincial governments and the cost is shared, it is important that any federal plans for future improvement of the provisions of this legislation should be the subject of consultation between the federal and provincial governments. If the provinces will agree to share the additional cost the federal government is prepared to increase the maximum assistance payment under the federal legislation to $75 a month. One question of special interest to the federal government is whether the age of eligibility under the old age assistance program can be lowered from 65 to 60 for widows and unmarried women.
